en: May that abode, which follows Gokula, which enchants the eyes of the gopīs, and whose guileless, sweet smile fills the lineage [of the Yadus], protect us. 1.
In the great lineage of the Moon, purified by the preeminent conduct of the sons of Pāṇḍu,
there was a sovereign of boundless majesty named Rāmarāja.
Then, like a supreme jewel composed of nectar arising from the ocean, Queen Gopī appeared; she became the heart-captivating companion of Murāri, just as radiance is to a gem.
This royal sage, who for a very long time stood at the forefront of those true to their word,
propitiated Veṅkaṭeśvara and obtained sons of extraordinary nature.
When those lords of the three worlds had been honored, Śrī Cinnatimmarāja—whose majesty illuminated the entire circle of the earth—prevailed like the Sun, the kinsman of the lotus. || 5 ||
The broad victory pillars situated there appear like stakes driven into the ocean by one crossing it, out of fear that the bridge might give way. (6)
Near the ridges of the Malaya mountains, his pillar of victory appears like the Vindhya range, emerging from its base as if to question Agastya: "Why have you not returned even today? (7)
The moon of his fame—born from the ocean of the water of charity and a wonder to the world—overcomes the dark clouds of time and eclipses the mass of the sun’s rays. (8)
That steadfast man, who always nourishes the wise with the nectars produced from his own eloquent verses, follows the conduct of the moon, the progenitor of his lineage.
Once, while presiding over a delightful literary assembly,
he heard the poem *Yādavābhyudaya* from the mouths of learned men.
Because it had not been explained by those who came before, its true nature remained unmanifested,
like a noble emerald that has not yet been polished by experts in the craft.
Then, my curiosity immediately aroused by Karna’s words, he appointed me to explain that [text] before the learned assembly. (12)
Out of great respect for the command of the protector of the earth, I shall explain this poem of the lion among poets and logicians according to my own understanding. (13)

In this regard, following the traditional rule that "the introduction to a work consists of a benediction, a salutation, or a statement of the subject matter" (Kāvyādarśa 1.14), the Teacher composes a benedictory verse at the outset, characterized by a salutation to his chosen deity:
"I pay homage to the one who wanders in Vṛndāvana, the beloved of the cowherd maidens, the light born of Jayantī, whose ornament is the Vaijayantī garland. (1)

"Vanda" refers to a specific forest named Vṛndāvana located near Mathurā; one who moves about there is a "vṛndāvanacaraḥ. The suffix *ṭa* is applied according to Pāṇini 3.2.16 (*careṣṭaḥ*). Regarding the elision of the case-ending (*supo luk*), although the rule for non-elision (*aluk*) in a *tatpuruṣa* compound with a *kṛt*-suffix (Pāṇini 6.3.14) is stated to be "frequently occurring" (*bāhulaka*), here the elision takes place by virtue of that frequent occurrence. "Vallavīs" are women of the cowherd caste; the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* is applied to the word *vallava* to denote a genus.

The term *vallavyaḥ* is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning "the people who are cowherds" (*vallavī-janāḥ*). Because there is no subsequent cause for the feminine gender, the word *vallavī* does not undergo the masculine substitution (*pumbhāva*) prescribed by rules such as *puṃvat karmadhāraye* (Pāṇini 6.3.42). Their beloved is that which is defined as follows: "He who, being himself full, assists through truthful speech, nobility, and self-restraint, and speaks kindly—he becomes dear to a woman. (Bhagavad Purāṇa 5.14.8). This is the "dear one."

"Beloved, dear, and cherished"—thus says Amara [AK 3.1.109]. Jayantī, conjoined with Rohiṇī, is the eighth day of the dark fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa. It is etymologically defined by the authors of the Purāṇas: "Because she extends victory (jaya) and merit (puṇya), they know her as Jayantī. The word is grammatically correct due to its inclusion in the *pṛṣodarādi* group. In that [Jayantī], there was a "manifestation" (*sambhavam*), derived from the root *bhū* with the suffix *ac* (pacādyac). This is according to the rule: "The suffix *ap* (which becomes *a*) is prescribed after all roots" [KV 3.1.134].

The compound is formed by means of a *yogavibhāga* (splitting of the rule) regarding the seventh case. The construction is as follows: "I salute"—that is, I bow down—to that abode known as Vāsudeva, which is characterized by having the Vaijayantī forest-garland as its ornament, and which consists of the light of self-luminous radiance. The use of the present tense in "I salute" (*vande*) is intended to indicate the perpetual continuation of one's own salutation, rather than merely referring to its occurrence at the specific time of commencing this treatise; for there is no reason for such a restriction.

Because the Lord, who grants all desired objects by the mere act of once taking refuge, is always followed by the mental salutation—which consists of a specific contemplation of Him—arising from the devotion of the virtuous; for, by the power of the qualifier alone, the Lord Vāsudeva is understood as the qualified object. Thus, there is no explicit mention of the qualified object. As Vāmana has said: "The use of the qualifier alone [suffices] when the qualified object is to be understood. (KAS 5.1.10)

The four qualities conducive to the Blessed One’s being easy to serve are: affection (*vātsalya*), good character (*sauśīlya*), accessibility (*saulabhya*), and lordship (*svāmitva*). Among these, *vātsalya* is affection like that of a cow for its calf. *Sauśīlya* is the nature of maintaining constant intimacy with even the lowly despite one's greatness. *Saulabhya* is the state of being easily attained and the quality of granting one's presence with ease. *Svāmitva* is the sense of ownership or the feeling of "mine" toward [his devotees].

Through *vātsalya* (parental affection), the servant’s fear of his own transgressions is removed; through *sauśīlya* (good character), the fear that the Supreme Lord is unapproachable due to His majesty is removed; through *saulabhya* (accessibility), the fear that He is beyond perception—arising from hearing Vedāntic statements such as “His form does not stand within the range of vision” (*PaU 19*)—is removed; and through *svāmitva* (lordship), the fear that there is no relationship rooted in *vātsalya* and the other qualities is removed. Thus, these qualities are useful for making Him easy to serve. These qualities are sequentially associated with the four epithets.

In this regard, by the first epithet, which describes his wandering through Vṛndāvana in the form of a cowherd following calves, his affection (*vātsalya*) common even to the animal species is manifested. In order to illuminate that for one who is eternally satisfied by the constant embrace of Śrī Mahālakṣmī—the foremost among all women—his embracing of women of the low-born cowherd class is caused solely by his noble character (*sauśīlya*), the second epithet uses the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* in the word "vallavī," thereby indicating their status as belonging to the cowherd caste.

Even by the word *jana*, which denotes common folk (*pāmara*), his excellent character (*sauśīlya*) is further confirmed. As the *Viśvaprakāśa* states: “The word *jana* is used in the world [to mean people], from Maharloka [upward], and in the sense of the next world (*paraloka*). Thus, the word *jana* itself possesses semantic significance. By the third epithet, through the mention of his form as an incarnation (*avatāra*), his accessibility (*saulabhya*) is suggested; for in passages such as “whose forms are incarnations,” the accessibility of incarnations is well-established.

By the fourth qualification, through the statement in the *Śrīmad Bhāgavata*: “He wears His own Māyā, called Vaijayantī, which consists of the three *guṇas*,” the nature of the Lord as the substratum of Māyā and the cause of the universe is revealed by establishing that Vaijayantī, who is of the nature of Māyā, serves as His ornament and attribute; thus, His lordship (*svāmitva*) is manifested. This is because of the scriptural testimony regarding His lordship over the individual souls (*jīvas*): “He is the cause, the Lord of the lords of the senses” (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.9).

By this very qualification, the fact that [the author] has the nature of Brahman, the cause of the universe, is implied; thus, the Lord’s qualities—such as omniscience and omnipotence—which are useful for performing his task, are also brought to mind. Because he is useful for this specific task at hand, namely the composition of this work, the Lord is invoked as "Dhāma" (the Abode), with an emphasis on his power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*). Furthermore, by these very qualifications, there is also provided an indication of the subject matter and the purpose of this poem, which are necessary for the engagement of discerning readers.

For instance: by the three qualifiers beginning with "wandering in Vṛndāvana," it is indicated that the subject matter (*viṣaya*) of this work is the Lord’s pastimes, such as his wandering in Vṛndāvana. By that very [description], because its nature as being filled with the sentiments (*rasa*) of erotic love (*śṛṅgāra*), heroism (*vīra*), and wonder (*adbhuta*) is made manifest, its purpose (*prayojana*)—which is the aesthetic relish (*āsvāda*) of those sentiments—is indicated. Furthermore, by employing the word *jayantī* in the phrase "born on Jayantī" (*jayantīsaṃbhavam*)—referring to the lunar day of the Lord's manifestation—the suggestion (*vyañjana*) of His victorious nature (*jayaśīlatva*) reveals that His life-story is permeated by the sentiment of heroism (*vīrarasa*).

In this context, the heroic sentiment (*vīrarasa*) is the predominant element, because the purpose of the incarnation is to remove the burden of the earth. To highlight its predominance, a qualifying attribute that suggests it—namely, “the splendor born of Jayantī”—is placed in proximity to the substantive. Thus, the intermediate purpose is manifested through these three qualifiers.

Furthermore, by the phrase "the ornament of Vaijayantī," which reveals Kṛṣṇa’s nature as the Supreme Brahman, the liberation (mukti) resulting from the poem's focus on the Supreme Brahman is indicated as being like the wages for eating sugarcane; this is because the constant contemplation of the Supreme Brahman culminates in liberation. Thus, because these adjectives possess a specific intended meaning, there is the poetic figure of speech known as *parikara*, which consists in the employment of adjectives with a deliberate purpose (*sābhiprāyaviśeṣaṇavinyāsa*).

In the phrases "I praise Bṛndā," "the beloved of the cowherd girls," "Jayantī," and "Vaijayantī," because of the equality of syllables (*varṇasamatva*), there is the figure of speech *anuprāsa* (alliteration) consisting of such syllabic equality. Since there is no restriction regarding the position that would necessitate *yamaka* (rhyme), there is no suspicion of *yamaka* anywhere here. By the use of the present tense in "I praise" (*vande*), the poet’s state of passion (*rati-bhāva*) directed toward the Lord is suggested according to the manner previously described; thus, this is *bhāva-dhvani* (suggestion of emotion).

Thus, by the very dignity of the hero, there is also suggested the worthiness of this poem composed by such a Great Man (mahāpuruṣa) through the dignity of its author; this is therefore a suggestion of a fact (*vastudhvani*). Furthermore, through the dignity of both the leader and the author, as well as the excellence of its fruit, the superiority of this poem over other poems of a different kind is suggested; this is also a suggestion of the figure of speech "contrast" (*vyatirekālaṃkāradhvani*). Moreover, the qualities (*guṇas*) such as clarity (*prasāda*) and the rest are to be observed in this verse according to their possibility.

The purity of the *gaṇa* and the phoneme is clearly established by the initial employment of the *magaṇa*, which has the Earth as its deity, and the syllable *va*, which is the seed-syllable of nectar (*amṛtabīja*). Although for the inhabitants of the North the verbal root *vand* begins with a labial, Bakipati stated in his *Bādhabandhatī*—under the heading "In the *Bhvādi* class, it begins with the third letter of the *pavarga*"—that it begins with the third letter of the *pavarga*.

Nevertheless, just as with the root *ślāgh* (in the sense of praising), although it ends in the third letter of the *ṭ*-class (*ḍ*) in the Dhātupāṭha, in common usage forms such as *rūpaśālī* and *bhāgyaśālī* appear with a *l*, because *ḍ* and *l* are identical; likewise, because *b* and *v* are identical, its usage in the world begins with a semivowel (*antasthādi*). However, in Mādhava’s *Dhātuvṛtti*, even in the Dhātupāṭha, it is accepted as beginning with a semivowel. Alternatively, this verse is intended as a formal declaration (*pratijñā*) for the commencement of the poem; in this view, *vande* means "I praise."

The present tense (*laṭ*) is used here according to the rule *vartamānasāmīpye* (Pāṇini 3.3.131), meaning "I shall praise" (*stoṣye*). Of the verbal root *vad*, which signifies both salutation and praise, the sense of praise is adopted here. Thus, the commencement of a poem consisting of praise—characterized by the recitation of the divine qualities of the Blessed One through the medium of His various deeds—is hereby promised. Furthermore, this verse is in the *yugmavipulā* meter; some maintain it is the *pathyāvaktra* meter.

“Wherein the seventh [syllable] occurs in both even [pādas], that is considered *yugmavipulā*. [VRK 2.25] “In the even [pādas], by means of the *ja* [syllable], the *pathyāvakra* of the Lord of Rivers is proclaimed. [VRK 2.22] Thus, it is because of the specific distinction in the aesthetic flavor (*vicchitti*) of both. || 1 ||
He who speaks the truth, delights in honesty, acts for another's benefit, and speaks kindly— such a man, being himself pleased, becomes beloved by a woman.
Since even the panegyrists of the Vedas are exhausted at the limit of describing each single quality,
what need is there to mention others who are limited in their knowledge?

One might object: "How is it possible to describe the qualities of the Blessed One, whose auspicious virtues are immeasurable and infinite? To this, he raises the objection with the words, "That which each... The *nigamas*—the Vedas themselves—are the *vandins*. They are called *vandins* because they necessarily praise (*vandante*) or extol some quality, whether real or unreal; thus, they are like panegyrists. The suffix *ṇini* is applied in the sense of necessity according to the rule *āvaśyakādhamarṇyayor ṇiniḥ* (Pāṇini 3.3.170), since the verbal root *vand* has the meaning of praising.

At the limit of each individual quality—that is, at the very pinnacle of each single quality of that Blessed One—others have become exhausted; having set out to praise Him, they were unable to describe even a single quality in its entirety and were thwarted at the very outset. This is the meaning. Of that Blessed One, in the description of His qualities exactly as they are and as they deserve—in a perfect description of His virtues—what need is there to mention those others who are limited and petty? The sense is: how much less are they capable? What more can be said?

The repetition in *ekaika* is for the sake of distributive emphasis (*vīpsā*). Due to the application of the rule *ekaṃ bahuvrīhivat* (Pāṇini 8.1.9), which treats the word as a *bahuvrīhi*, the case-ending (*sup*) is elided. In the word *yathāvat*, the suffix *vati* is added after the word *yathā* in the sense of fitness (*arha*), according to the rule *tadarham* (Pāṇini 5.1.117). In the word *mitampacāḥ*, the suffix *khaś* is applied to the root *pac* by the rule *mitanakhe ca* (Pāṇini 3.2.34); the augment *mum* is then inserted by the rule *arurdviṣadajantasya mum* (Pāṇini 6.3.67).

"‘*Kadarya*, *kṛpaṇa*, *kṣudra*, *kiṃpacāna*, and *mitampaca*’—thus says Amara. This is the sense: even the Vedas, which are like bards whose nature is to praise by superimposing qualities upon other deities such as Indra—even though those qualities do not exist in them—in the manner of ‘O Indra, there is none higher than you; O Rudra, you are higher than all,’ have set about praising His qualities throughout the flow of beginningless and endless time.”

Even those who have grown weary at the very limit of each single quality—whose excellence is understood through the various deeds performed by Him throughout immeasurable kalpas—are unable to fully record even a mere fraction of a crore of His life-stories; so what need is there to mention that petty men, incapable of describing even a tiny fragment of virtue found among humans and others, would exhaust themselves in attempting to describe the fullness of His own possession of all virtues?

Here, at the commencement of his poem, the poet has presented a general statement while intending to demonstrate his own lack of ability in order to manifest his humility; thus, because the specific subject at hand is understood from this general statement that is not the primary subject, there is *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise). Because of the introduction of the *kaimutika* maxim by means of the word "kimuta," there is *arthāpatti* (presumption). Because of the superimposition of identity in the phrase "nigamavandinaḥ" (those who praise the Vedas), there is *rūpaka* (metaphor). And since these figures of speech mutually sustain one another, there is *saṃkara* (commixture).

Although in the expression *nigamavandinaḥ* ("those who praise the Vedas"), a comparative compound (*upamitasamāsa*)—meaning "the Vedas are like panegyrists"—is also possible according to the rule *upamitaṃ vyāghrādibhiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.56), nevertheless, because of the connection with "exertion" (*śrama*), it is determined to be a metaphorical identification (*rūpaka*), specifically a *mayūravyaṃsakādi* compound in which the meaning of the second member is predominant. For in a comparative compound, since the meaning of the first member is predominant, the connection with exertion would not apply to the primary sense [of the Vedas]. || 2 ||
It is appropriate that even those of dull intellect should find the taste of stories concerning Śauri within their power;
for if nectar were obtainable, would it not be seized by men? (3)

He resolves this objection with the words "śakyeti" (it is possible). Even for those of dull intellect (*mandadhiyām*), that is, those of small intelligence; "by capacity" (*śaktyā*) means to the best of one's ability. "The relish of the story of Śauri": Śauri is Kṛṣṇa, the offspring of Vasudeva, the father of Śūra; the suffix *iñ* is applied because the group beginning with *bāhu* is treated as an *ākṛtigaṇa*. According to the rule "only one [descendant] in a lineage" (*eko gotre*, Pāṇini 4.1.93), even when the descendant is removed by several generations, the suffix is applied directly to the original stem itself. The "relish" (*āsvāda*) of his story consists in its composition. It is "fitting" (*sthāne*), meaning appropriate.

“*Sthāne* means ‘in a fitting place’ or ‘appropriate’; this is from the *Ratnamālā*. He provides an illustration for this: ‘If nectar were obtainable, why would it not be grasped by men?’—the meaning is that it certainly would be tasted. [The use of the optative suffix] *liṅ* here follows Pāṇini 3.3.156: ‘*liṅ* is used for cause and effect. The intended sense is this: even though it is impossible to describe the qualities of the Blessed One in their entirety, a description to the extent of the power of one’s intellect to reach them is entirely appropriate, even for those of dull wit.”

However, one should not disregard even that portion which can be grasped by the power of describing it to the best of one's ability. For it is not the case that because mortals do not obtain much nectar, they do not taste whatever little they have obtained. Or rather, the intention is this: just as when nectar is obtained, humans do not discard it themselves, thinking "this is fit for the gods," but rather they certainly taste what has been obtained; so too should it be here.

Thus, although they are not authorized to describe the totality of the Lord’s qualities due to their dull-wittedness, those who possess the discernment of aesthetic flavor (*rasajña*) and are wise do not remain indifferent, thinking, "This is the task of others"; rather, they indeed describe whatever portion is possible for them. Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever in my undertaking the description of the Lord’s deeds according to my own intellect. Here, as before, the figure of speech is *aprastutapraśaṃsā* (indirect praise).

Because there is a connection between the common attributes of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*)—both of which consist of the nectar of the Blessed One’s life—and because these two distinct things are presented in two separate sentences through the relationship of prototype and reflection (*bimbapratibimbabhāva*), this is an *dṛṣṭānta* (illustration). Furthermore, since the word "tasting" (*āsvāda*) involves a suppressed identification (*nigīryādhyavasāna*) of the connection [between the two], it constitutes the figure of speech *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) in the form of identity despite difference. Moreover, by means of this suppressed identification, the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) based on metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇāmūla*) is that [the life-story] is an object of excessive longing;
and since this enhances the aforementioned illustration, it is a variety of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion). || 3 ||
While he, born from the ear of the Earth, was present and Vyāsa remained in his heart,
other poets indeed became shameless at will.

Regarding the word *vasudhā*: *vasudhā-śrotra* means "the anthill," for the *Ratnakośa* states in its synonyms for anthill (*valmīka*): "The anthill is *vāmalūra* and *bhūśravaḥ*. The Vedic scripture (*Śruti*) also says: "For this anthill is the ear of the earth" (TB 1.1.1.3–4). Born there is *vasudhā-śrotraja*, namely Vālmīki; the suffix *ḍa* is applied according to the rule *saptamyāṃ janer ḍaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.2.97). The sense is that he composed such a famous first poem (*ādikāvya*) as that.

And while Vyāsa, the compiler of the Mahābhārata, remains present within the heart and manifests in the mind, others as well—even those distinct from both of them—will certainly be utterly devoid of shame (*anapatrapāḥ*). Seeing the *Rāmāyaṇa* and the *Mahābhārata*, they will look upon their own compositions; how could they not be laughed at? Thus, they are simply lacking in shame toward others. As Amara states: "Mandākṣa, hrī, trapā, brīḍā, and lajjā denote shame; sāpatrapā denotes shame before others. (Amara-kośa 1.7.455).

Poets were indeed creators of poetry. Even after seeing the compositions of Vyāsa and Vālmīki, the inclination of others toward the independent composition of their own works was nothing but a shameless act; thus, this verse is intended to praise those two. Alternatively, since the compositions of the great poets of old already exist, this verse serves to manifest one's own modesty by avoiding the impropriety of engaging in the composition of one’s own work. In this latter sense, the word *anye* means "others besides me."

The intended meaning is this: for just as other poets have composed their works based upon the *Rāmāyaṇa* and the *Mahābhārata* even though those [epics] already existed, so too is this being composed by me. What shame is there in composing according to one's own intellect? (4)

He is called a poet, a creator, in whom the Goddess of Speech delights through figures of speech—whether they consist of rasa, bhāva, or subordinate elements—as well as through the manifestation of poetic qualities. (5)

Regarding the word "sa" (that): *rasas* are the erotic and other aesthetic sentiments (*śṛṅgārādi*); *bhāvas* are the determinants (*vibhāva*), consequents (*anubhāva*), and transitory states (*sañcārī*) appropriate to those respective sentiments; *guṇībhūtavyaṅgyas* are suggested meanings that have attained a subordinate status due to reasons such as being non-recondite (*agūḍha*), being a limb of another (*aparāṅga*), being a factor for the realization of the expressed meaning (*vācyasiddhyaṅga*), being indistinct (*asphuṭa*), having equal prominence with the expressed meaning (*tulyaprādhānya*), being implied by intonation (*kākvākṣipta*), or being unpleasant (*asundara*), as stated in the verse: “Non-recondite, a limb of another, a factor for the realization of the expressed, indistinct, those of equal prominence, implied by intonation, and the unpleasant. By these, and by *alaṅkāras* such as alliteration (*anuprāsa*) and simile (*upamā*).

"Characterized by those modes" means characterized by those ways in which the emergence of qualities (*guṇodayāḥ*)—namely, the manifestation through specific phonemes, compounds, and stylistic structures of qualities such as sweetness (*mādhurya*) and others inherent in aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)—is revealed. "The Bhāratī" refers to speech. "Wherein she delights" means that wherein she exists in the form of an unrestrained flow, by her own accord and without being forcibly drawn. "That creator" is the producer, through his intuition (*pratibhā*), of a subject matter not previously delineated by other poets.

The primary meaning is that "kavi" is called a poet, or is designated as such. Furthermore, in this context, there are the *rasas* and *bhāvas* impelled by passion (*rāga*), whose *anubhāvas*—such as glances toward the eyes and gentle smiles—are manifested through *alaṅkāras*, namely ornaments like bracelets and armlets (which serve as embellishments), and through *guṇas*, namely beauty, youth, and so forth. These are called "arising" (*udaya*) because they emerge upon seeing the hero; these include the transformations of the gaze and other such signs. By means of these, [the *rasas* and *bhāvas*] flourish. This is the sense. They are further enhanced by those qualities which have become subordinate (*guṇībhūta*) and which serve as the causes for their full manifestation. Thus, the *rasas* and *bhāvas* are brought to perfection. This is the intended meaning. It is not the case that the *rasas* and *bhāvas* are merely subordinate to the *alaṅkāras* and *guṇas*. Rather, it is the *alaṅkāras* and *guṇas* that are subordinate to the *rasas* and *bhāvas*. This is because the *rasas* and *bhāvas* are the primary objects to be expressed, while the *alaṅkāras* and *guṇas* are the means by which they are expressed. Therefore, the *rasas* and *bhāvas* are the principal elements, and the *alaṅkāras* and *guṇas* are subordinate. This is the established rule. For example, in the verse beginning with "The moon has risen," the *rasa* is the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), and the *bhāva* is longing (*autsukya*). The *anubhāvas* are the glances and so forth. The *guṇas* are beauty, youth, and so on. The *alaṅkāras* are the bracelet, the armlet, and so forth. All these are subordinate to the *rasa* and *bhāva*. This is the intended meaning. Furthermore, in the verse beginning with "O friend, look at the moon," the *rasa* is the erotic, and the *bhāva* is longing. The *anubhāvas* are the glances and so forth. "The qualities of the object, its activities, its ornaments, and those that are neutral—these are to be known as the fourfold sequence of excitants (*uddīpana*). [Nāṭyaśāstra 7.32] It has been stated that the qualities, ornaments, and activities of the heroine serve as the causes for exciting the state of passion (*rati-bhāva*) in the hero. Such is the Goddess of Speech (*Bhāratī Vāgdevatā*), in whom he delights—that is, she brings him joy. He, the creator and fashioner of the worlds, the Four-faced One, is designated as the "Poet" (*kavi*).

By the statement, "He who [revealed] the Veda to the first poet with his heart" (BhP 1.1.1), the subject under discussion is understood. And just as the four-faced Brahmā is designated as a 'poet' (kavi) because he is the abode of Sarasvatī’s sport, so too one who possesses poetry characterized by the aforementioned form is designated as a 'poet'; thus, the figure of speech known as *upamā* (simile) is suggested (*dhvani*).

By this composition of such poetry—which is devoid of the aesthetic charm (*camatkāra*) of rasa, bhāva, and so forth—it is suggested that poets who subsist on the leftovers of others do not truly exist as poets. Since the denial of their status as poets is logically untenable, it culminates in a specific quality, namely their ridiculousness; thus, the figure of speech *ākṣepa* (paralipsis), which consists in the appearance of a denial intended to highlight a desired particularity, is here suggested (*dhvanita*).

By this self-reproach of bad poets, he demonstrates the maturity of his own poetry through the declaration "I am not such [as they]," thereby revealing his modesty in the preceding verse so that no suspicion may arise regarding the insignificance of his authorship. Thus, by being replete with rasa, bhāva, and other elements, the superior quality of his poem is illuminated; consequently, a succession of *dhvani*s—consisting of both *vastu-dhvani* and *alaṅkāra-dhvani* rooted in the power of words (*śabdaśaktimūla*)—is to be discerned. || 5 ||
At present, everything is new, and in the future, it will all be old;
neither of these two states conduces to either fault or virtue.

Now, he addresses those dull-witted people who might point out the fault that his own poem is merely "new" by saying: "In its own time," and so forth. "All" refers to the entire collection of compositions, both present-day and ancient. "In its own time" (tadātve) means at that very moment; it is "new. "In the future" (āyatyaṃ), meaning at a later time, it is "ancient. The word *ca* (and) is placed out of its logical order (*bhinnakramaḥ*), serving to conjoin two attributes in a single instance. Amara states: "The term *tadātva* denotes that very time, while *āyati* denotes a subsequent time. (Amarakośa 2.7.990).

Both of these—novelty and antiquity—are neither conducive to fault nor conducive to merit. According to the rule, “the fourth case is used for that which is being rendered fit” (*Pāṇini* 5.4.50), that very thing which is desired to be censured as novel becomes ancient in the course of time; and that which is desired to be adopted as ancient is likewise novel in its own time. Therefore, the sense is that these two do not serve as the grounds for rejection or adoption in literary compositions, but rather depend solely on the deficiency or completeness of their respective characteristics. O sinless one, even when she falters at times while proceeding on her path,
they do not disregard her speech, just as connoisseurs do not disregard a dancer.

"Engaged" (*pravṛttām*): *Agha* means sin or evil; as Ajaya states, "The word *agha* may refer to sin, as well as to suffering and calamity. That which is contrary to this is *anagha* (sinless). This is a negative compound (*nañ-samāsa*). In that non-contradictory [path], which effects the destruction of all sins—that path consisting of the composition of the Lord’s deeds—I have engaged my speech, that is, my poetic composition. In some instances, regarding subtle subjects such as the secrets of the Lord’s life, or regarding the merits and defects of words and meanings.

"Even those who are negligent and inattentive"—the word *bhāvukāḥ* means devotees of the Blessed One (*bhagavadbhaktāḥ*) produced by contemplation (*bhāvanākṛtaḥ*). The suffix *ukañ* is applied to the root *bhū* after its causative form (*ṇijanta*), according to the rule "bhuvo ’vakalkane" (Dhātupāṭha 10.207), as well as the rule "lapapatādibhya ukañ" (Pāṇini 3.2.154).

"Avakalkana" has been explained as "thinking. They do not disregard [the scripture] even out of mere negligence; they do not treat the *tantra* with contempt, but rather accept it—however loosely composed it may be—with regard to its subject, the Blessed One, as that which destroys all sins. Thus it is said in the Śrīmad Bhāgavatam: "That utterance of words is a flood that washes away the sins of the people, in which [even if it is] loosely composed in every verse..."

"The virtuous hear, sing, and praise the names of Ananta, which are marked by his glory" (BhP 1.5.11). The phrase "like a dancer" (*nartakīm iva*) is an indication of a simile. In this context, *anaghe* means "O sinless one," who, through the tasting of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) of the drama in which all other objects of knowledge have dissolved, is opposed to suffering. Regarding the term *mārge*: in the treatises on music (*saṅgīta*), dance is said to be of two kinds—*mārga* and *deśī*. Here, it refers to the dance called *mārga*. Thus, she is like a dancer engaged in *mārga-nṛtta*, or like a woman who has received training in the *mārga* style of dance.

“A dancer (*nartaka*) is said to be fragrant (*surabhi*) when he has exerted effort in the performance of the *mārga* dance,” according to the *Saṅgītaratnākara*. By applying the suffix *ṣvun* according to *Pāṇini 3.1.145* (*śilpini ṣvun*), and then the feminine suffix *ṅīṣ* according to *Pāṇini 4.1.41* (*ṣidgaurādibhyaś ca*), we derive the form *bhāvukāḥ*, meaning those who know the specific gestures and expressions (*bhāva-ceṣṭā-viśeṣa*) of each [sentiment]. Śāradātanaya states: “Sentiments (*bhāva*) are never perceived without gestures; therefore, those who know the specific gestures are known as *bhāvukas*, connoisseurs (*rasika*). (*Bharatārṇava-prakāśa* 6).

Here, because the words "path" (*mārga*) and "those who cultivate" (*bhāvukāḥ*)—which have distinct meanings—are uttered simultaneously, there is *śleṣa* (paronomasia). Furthermore, for the purpose of establishing the common attribute (*sāmānyadharma*) between the two meanings conveyed by the paronomastic words within a simile, there is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) based on the identification (*abhedādhyavasāya*) [of the two meanings]. And this is further vitalized by the figure of speech *upamā* (simile) in the phrase "like a dancer" (*nartakīm iva*). || 7 ||
Casting aside that shame, I shall proclaim the rise of Vasudeva’s son— the nectar of the ocean of Vyāsa’s words and the life-sustenance of the wise.

"Vihāya" means: for that reason, from the cause already stated. "Vihāya" means having cast aside shame (*vrīḍā*) and the embarrassment (*trapā*) of thinking, "They will mock me by relying on some triviality. "Vyāsavedārṇavāmṟtam": The *Vyāsa-veda* is the *Mahābhārata*; it is an ocean, and its "nectar" (*amṛta*) is like nectar, being its essential essence. "Vibudhāḥ" refers to the learned; they are themselves the "gods" (*vibudhāḥ*), which is a punning metaphor (*śliṣṭarūpaka*). For them, it is the "sustenance" (*jīvātu*), meaning both their food and their life-restoring medicine. For the gods, nectar is the food; for the learned, this literary composition is [the sustenance].

Because it enters the heart, it is so called by way of metaphor. Viśva [the lexicographer] states: *“Jīvātu means life; jīvātu is a medicinal herb for living.”* I shall speak—that is, I shall express or describe—the *udaya*, meaning the exaltation, of Kṛṣṇa, the son of Vasudeva. The root *brū* (to speak) is used here in the middle voice (*ātmanepada*) with the suffix *va*. Here, there is a combination (*saṅkara*) of two metaphors (*rūpaka*) based on both paronomastic (*śliṣṭa*) and non-paronomastic (*aśliṣṭa*) words: “the nectar of the ocean of Vyāsa’s Vedas” and “the life-restorer (*jīvātu*) of the wise. || 8 ||
By means of his own playful brush, stained with compassion,
the one, all-pervading, and glorious Lord himself produced this manifold painting of the universe.

Now, because it is remembered that hearing the lineage of Yadu is supremely purifying—as stated in the verse: “When a person hears the lineage of Yadu, he is liberated from all sins; therein descended the one called Kṛṣṇa, the perfect Brahman in human form” (VP 4.11.4)—the author, desiring to describe the deeds of the Blessed Lord after first narrating the succession of the Yadu dynasty, intends to declare the birth of the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) from the mind of Candra, the progenitor of the Yadu lineage, according to the method of the *Puruṣasūkta*.

As an introduction to that [subject], the Blessed One, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), first states the point that "all this world was created" with the word *krīḍā* (play). The term *vibhuḥ* means one who possesses unsurpassed majesty due to being endowed with various powers conducive to the creation, preservation, and destruction of the entire universe. The term *śrīmān* contains the possessive suffix *matup* in the sense of eternal connection; thus, the Supreme Person is eternally joined with the imperishable Śrī Mahālakṣmī. The term *ekaḥ* means precisely without dependence on any other assistant. *Idam* refers to this entire universe or the whole world.

"Viśva" means "of the entire world. "Citra" refers to that which is wonderful or marvelous; thus, "citra" is a *śliṣṭarūpaka* (a punning metaphor), for it signifies both a painting and a marvel. As Amarasimha states: "The word *citra* denotes both a painting (*ālekhya*) and a marvel (*āścarya*). With a playful brush—the very play itself being the brush, the tool for painting—smeared with the pigment of compassion, namely the essence of mercy, he himself, acting as an independent agent, produced [the world] within himself, taking his own self as the substratum. He brought it into existence.

The form [of the verb] is from the root *jan* (to be born) with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in the aorist (*luṅ*). The use of the aorist is intended to express the general past tense. Here, by means of the two qualifiers "himself" (*svayam*) and "in himself" (*sve*), the Blessed One’s twofold nature as both the efficient and material cause of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is demonstrated. To manifest his lack of any equal or superior, it is shown that the creation of this phenomenal world, composed of many millions of universes, occurs without dependence on any other auxiliary, by the word "one" (*ekam*).

In order to dispel the doubt regarding the impossibility of [the Lord] being the agent of the creation of this manifold universe while being without assistance, it is shown that he possesses all powers by the word "vibhu" (all-pervading). For the term "vibhu," when free from the limitations of context or qualifying words, proclaims his unsurpassed majesty. To ward off the suspicion that the creation of the manifold universe is untenable for the Blessed One—who has eternally attained all desires—due to a lack of purpose, it is stated: "by means of the brush of play."

Just as a sovereign emperor, though having all his desires fulfilled, might playfully engage in games such as ball-play, so too does the Blessed Lord [engage in the world]; this is the intended meaning regarding His sport with the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). Now, one might raise the objection: "If He plunges the multitudes of living beings into the mire of suffering—such as dwelling in hells or wombs—merely for the sake of His own sport, then He would be utterly merciless. Consequently, His perfection in all auspicious qualities and His being the opposite of everything that is to be rejected would be lost. To ward off this doubt, it is said: "by [sport] colored by compassion" (*kṛpārūṣitayā*).

He does not create the world merely as a matter of sport (*līlā*), but rather through one colored by compassion (*kṛpā*). For this very reason, even those portions of the Veda that set forth the means to liberation have been taught; likewise, the rituals conducive to that end, and the rice and other grains required to perform them, were created. Indeed, if He lacked sincere and unsurpassed compassion for living beings, He—a being eternally satisfied—would not Himself teach the rituals and other means to liberation. Furthermore, although He possesses sincere compassion, He does not liberate [beings] without cause.

The sense is that there would otherwise result an absolute contradiction with His own divine play (*svalīlā*); furthermore, even the Lord who grants liberation is dependent upon the *dharma* that serves as the means to liberation, and thus He is subject neither to partiality (*vaiṣamya*) nor to cruelty (*nairghṛṇya*), according to the principle: “There is no partiality or cruelty, because He is dependent [on the merit of souls]” (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.34). Now, when the question arises—“What is the proof that the Creator of such a world is indeed Puruṣottama?”—the author states “the Glorious One” (*śrīmān*) in order to demonstrate that the *Puruṣasūkta* is the authority for this point.

Indeed, Puruṣottama alone is renowned as the Lord of Śrī. Furthermore, in the subsequent section immediately following the *Puruṣasūkta*, which forms a single syntactical unit with it, the status of being the Lord of Śrī is attributed to that very Puruṣa—the creator of the universe—in the passage: "Hrī and Lakṣmī are your two wives" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.13.2). Therefore, the intention is that Puruṣottama alone is established as the creator of the world. Thus should all things be contemplated at every step.

Even in the elegant poems of the lion among poets and logicians, such details are not elaborated here for fear of excessive prolixity; rather, the method of ancient commentators on poetry is followed. Thus, because both the adjectives and the substantive possess intentional significance (*sābhiprāyatva*), there are the two figures of speech *parikara* and *parikarāṅkura*. The distinction between them is that *parikara* consists in the intentional significance of the adjectives, while *parikarāṅkura* consists in the intentional significance of the substantive. The expression "with the brush of play" (*krīḍātūlikayā*) is a metaphor (*rūpaka*).

Furthermore, by means of the metaphorical attribution (*āropa*) of being a "cotton mattress" (*tūlikā*) to her play (*krīḍā*), based on its conformity with the nature of form (*rūpaṇā*), the attribution of being a "saffron-paste" (*rūṣikā*)—that is, a substance of passion (*rāga*)—to her compassion (*kṛpā*) is understood; thus, there is the figure of speech known as *ekadeśavṛtti-rūpaka* (metaphor occurring in one part). And since this metaphor gives rise to a punning metaphor (*śliṣṭa-rūpaka*) in the word "painting" (*citra*), there is a commingling (*saṃkara*) of these two figures through that [latter]. || 9 ||

From his mind was born Candramas, the delighter of the world,
like grace personified for those who were to be protected.

"Of that Puruṣottama," [it is said] "the world. From his mind—that is, from his mental essence—was born the Moon, the delighter of the world, who brings joy to all people; the suffix *lyuṭ* is used here in the sense of the agent due to the inclusion of the word *bahula*. He was like the personified grace of his mind, or like the mass of virtues such as gratitude. He was born (*jajñe*), meaning he came into being; this is the perfect tense (*liṭ*) of the root *jan* in the active voice. The elision of the penultimate vowel occurs according to the rule: "In the case of *kṅit* affixes, except for *anaṅ*, there is elision of the penultimate vowel in the roots *gam*, *han*, *jan*, *khan*, and *ghas*" (Pāṇini 6.4.98).

The poetic figure here is *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy), because the moon’s nature as the delighter of the world and so forth leads to the imaginative identification of it with the clarity of the Lord’s mind. Śāradātanaya states: “Gratitude, the quality of being a benefactor, and the further absence of faults—this is declared by those who know the characteristics to be the definition of the clarity of minds. {1} Although in the *Śrī Viṣṇupurāṇa* and other texts, his descent from Atri is mentioned at the beginning of the Lunar Dynasty (*Candravaṃśa*);

Nevertheless, in order to demonstrate the excellence of the noble lineage of the kings of the Lunar dynasty, the very procedure of the *Puruṣasūkta*—namely, "The Moon was born from the mind" (*candramā manaso jātaḥ*)—has been followed here. Nor should any contradiction be suspected in this regard; for there is no conflict, as his birth occurs in both cases according to different cycles of time (*samaya*). For it is said in the *Vāyavīya*: "The great seers have composed those various accounts concerning the events of their respective Kalpas; the wise man is not deluded by them. (10)

This has been declared as the characteristic of those with serene minds:
that Purūravas, whose merit and fame arose from his offspring,
became the presiding authority over the dwellings of the virtuous who maintain the sacred fires.

Regarding the word *yadapatya*: he was born from that which is the offspring (*apatya*) of the Moon (*candramas*), namely Budha. He is so described as one whose fame (*kīrti*) is meritorious—that is, merit-making (*puṇyakarī*). From the word *puṇya*, by adding the causative suffix *ṇic* (meaning "he makes it meritorious") and then the suffix *ac* (by *pacādyac*), followed by the elision of the *ṇic* according to Pāṇini 6.4.51 (*ṇer aniṭi*), the word *puṇya* comes to signify "merit-making. Such was Purūravas. [He was among] those who have established the sacred fires (*āhitavahni*), that is, those who maintain the fires (*āhitāgni*), and among the virtuous (*satām*), that is, the refined (*śiṣṭa*).

He attained the status of a *stheya*—one who decides upon a point of dispute—in the abode that exists after time, namely the abode of the next world (*paraloka-vihāra*). A *stheya* is one in whom a dispute is settled; as the *Viśva* lexicon states: "A *stheya* is a domestic priest who decides upon the subject matter of a dispute. Thus, it is heard in the *Viṣṇu Purāṇa* concerning Purūravas: "Following the tradition of the sacred scriptures (*āmnāya*), he offered oblations into the three fires produced by friction, having aimed for the fruit of dwelling in the same world as Urvaśī."

"By means of that very fire, having performed various sacrifices and attained the world of the Gandharvas, he obtained non-separation from Urvaśī. Fire was originally one; it was set forth in three ways during the Manvantara of Aila. This is the meaning: thus Purūravas became an authoritative witness for the virtuous regarding the correspondence between actions and their resulting fruits or lack thereof. Alternatively, this may be construed as *praṇayana*, meaning the carrying forward of the fires by dividing them into forms such as the Āhavanīya and others during the ritual performance (*vihāra*).

In passages such as *agniṃ vihṛtya*, the word *vihāra* is used in the sense of *praṇayana* (the formal leading forth of the fire). Thus, the meaning is that [the author] became an authoritative source for the conceptualization of the fires. In the phrase *yad apatya*, the word *yat* is connected with the preceding verse, *sa candramā jajñe*. Because the quality of being a judge (*stheyatva*) is superimposed upon what is not a judge (*astheya*), there is the poetic figure of *rūpaka* (metaphor). || 11 ||
That lineage grew higher and higher with successive generations,
by whose pearls of glory the ten directions were adorned.

"Samavardhata" (it grew). His lineage—that lineage, the progeny of that Moon—is itself a bamboo staff (*vaṃśa*). "Higher and higher" means successively upward. By means of the kings born in the manner beginning with Purūravas’s son Āyu, and from him Nahuṣa, and so forth—who are metaphorically determined to be mountains by their very mountain-like nature—the lineage grew, meaning it increased perfectly. Of that lineage, the glories themselves are the pearls; by those [glories].

The ten directions consist of the eight directions beginning with the east, plus above and below—these are the ten directions. "Adorned" means decorated. It is well known that pearls are produced from bamboo stalks. The phrase "that bamboo grew" connects with what precedes. Regarding the word *yat* occurring in the subsequent sentence, as is the case in *kulaka* verses, it connects with the preceding sentence even without the requirement of using the word *tat*; therefore, *tat* is not employed here.

This has been stated in the *Kāvyaprakāśikā*: “When the word *yat* is employed as referring to the meaning of a subsequent sentence, it does not require the explicit mention of the word *tat* referring to the meaning of the preceding sentence, by virtue of [semantic] capacity. Here, since being adorned is possible only by means of pearl-ornaments (*muktāphala*), there is a metaphorical compound (*rūpaka-samāsa*). When the pun (*śleṣa*) on the word *vaṃśa* is evoked by that, there arises the figure of speech known as *paraṃparita-rūpaka* (metaphor based on a series), which is grounded in the use of words with double meanings (*śliṣṭa-śabda*). || 12 ||
Nahuṣa became like Airāvata in that ocean;
upon Indra's departure, the gods installed him in his place.

"He became" means: in that lineage, Nahuṣa became like Airāvata in the ocean, the sea. When Indra, Śakra, had departed—that is, upon the departure of that Indra—the gods, Agni and the others, installed him in his place, in his station. [The form] *nyavīviśan* is derived from the root *viś* with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) in the aorist (*luṅ*). This is the figure of speech known as *upamā* (simile).

The story from the *Bhārata* should be recalled here: when Śakra had vanished somewhere, his power destroyed due to the sin of brahmin-murder resulting from the killing of Tvaṣṭṛ’s son, the other gods deliberated together and consecrated Nahuṣa—who was ruling the kingdom on earth, a performer of a hundred sacrifices, and deemed worthy of that position—in his place. In the compound *indravigama*, it is appropriate to refer to Indra, even though he is a subordinate member of the compound, by means of the pronoun *tasya*;
as Vāmana says: "A connection with a pronoun occurs for that which is concealed by a compound" (*vṛtticchannasya*). (13)
The lords of men on the circle of the earth, adorned with the marks of his name, became like moving victory pillars for that hero. (14)

"Kings": those kings—the other rulers—adorned with the name-signs of that hero Nahuṣa, meaning by bearing his name as a mark of having been conquered by him. "In the circle of the earth" (*pṛthivīcakra*) means on the terrestrial globe; according to the *Vaijayantī*: "The word *cakra* [denotes] an army, a whirlpool, a wheel, a multitude, a kingdom, a worldly existence, a circle, a hole, a division, and a type of weapon. "Moving" means mobile. They became like pillars of victory.

The sense is that even victory pillars are adorned with marks consisting of the inscription of the names of conquerors. Here, based on the quality of being marked with the names of kings, there is the figure of speech *svarūpotprekṣā* (poetic fancy of essential nature), which consists in the imagining of these [elephants] as mobile victory pillars. || 14 ||
Another reading: "The kings, adorned with the name-insignia of that hero, became like moving victory pillars upon the circle of the earth."
His power, unimpeded even by his enemies, was praised;
it was like the goddess Sarasvatī, who grants all that is desired to a practitioner according to the rules.

"Power" (śaktiḥ): belonging to that Nahuṣa; "unobstructed" (apratighā), meaning devoid of resistance (*pratighāta*). In the alternative sense of Sarasvatī, it means devoid of anger (*ruṭ*); for the *Vaijayantī* lexicon states, "Both *pratigha* and *pratighāta* mean anger" (*ruṭ*). "Power" (*śaktiḥ*) means strength. "Even by the enemies," that is, by rival kings, "was praised" (*tuṣṭuve*), meaning lauded; this is the periphrastic perfect (*liṭ*) in the passive voice (*karmaṇi*). "Properly" (*yathāvat*) means correctly. "Of the proponent" (*sādhakasya*), that is, of the disputant who establishes his own position.

It is as meaningful as it is complete, conveying every point that ought to be established, like the goddess Sarasvatī herself. For even here, when a discussion is being presented without dogmatism, the proponent is indeed praised immediately after by the opponents—even those who were previously offering clear praise—out of fear of defeat. This is the figure of speech known as *upamā* (simile). 15.
From Nahuṣa was born a hero named Yayāti, who, like the essence of energy itself,
occupied half the throne of Indra.

"Vīra" (the hero): from Nahuṣa was born Yayāti by name—Yayāti being well-known as such; for the *Ratnamālā* states, "The word *nāma* is used in the senses of manifestation and probability. From "utsāha" (enthusiasm), which is the *sthāyibhāva* (permanent emotion), there was born "vīra," like the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) called heroic. For it is recorded that "the excellence of emotion is known as *rasa*"; thus, because *rasa* is understood to be a particular state of the *sthāyibhāva*, there is here an expression of the causal relationship between the two. By that Yayāti, [he attained] that which pertains to Indra (*aindra*).

"Half-seat" (ardhāsana) means half of a seat; the compound is formed according to the rule "ardhaṃ napuṃsakaṃ" [Pāṇini 2.2.2]. "Occupied" (adhiṣṭhita) means sat down. One should here recall the story from the Mahābhārata regarding how Yayāti long occupied half the throne of Indra. This is the figure of speech known as simile (upamā). || 16 ||
Between his broad, expansive, and lofty shoulders,
the Earth herself sat upon half of his throne together with the Goddess of Heroic Splendor.

"Vishālā" means vast, extensive, wide, broad, lofty, and elevated; this is a descriptive compound (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*) like "lame-and-bent" (*khañjakubja*). According to the *Viśvakośa*: "The word *vipula* denotes breadth and the western mountain of Meru. Thus it is. In such a place—within the space between the shoulders (*bāhuśikhara*), that is, the region of the shoulders (*skandha*)—of that Yayāti, as Amara states: "The shoulder (*skandha*) is the top of the arm (*bhujaśiras*), also called *asa* (masculine/neuter). There, the Earth remained upon half the throne together with the glory of heroism (*vīraśrī*).
The meaning is that both the goddess of valor and the earth rested upon the very tip of his arm. || 17 ||

The word *taṭāka* is well known as ending in the *ka*-group (*kavarga*). [ST_1.10] “If those causes, effects, and concomitant factors that exist in the world for a permanent emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) such as love (*rati*) are, in drama and poetry, called excitants (*vibhāva*), ensuants (*anubhāva*), and transitory states (*vyabhicārin*); [KP_27-28] {1} In this regard, *rati* (love) is the permanent emotion of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*). "Despair, languor, apprehension, fatigue, dullness, joy, dejection, ferocity, anxiety, fear, envy, indignation, pride, recollection, death, intoxication, sleep, drowsiness, awakening, shame, epilepsy, delusion, equanimity, lassitude, impetuosity, deliberation, dissimulation, disease, madness, despondency, longing, and agitation—these thirty-three transitory states (sañcārin), when occurring alongside the stable emotion of love (rati) as its underlying persistence, exclude only lassitude, ferocity, and death. It has been stated that in this manner, for each individual rasa, its corresponding determinants (vibhāvas) and other factors are established; thus they are "fit" (bhavyāḥ).
