In the meantime, the goddess who has the ocean as her girdle spoke to the gods headed by Prajāpati, who had gone to the center of Mount Meru.

"In this" (*etasmin*): in this interval, at this opportunity. "The ocean-girdled" (*sāgaramekhalā*): the goddess Earth, whose girdle is the ocean. "To Meru's center": to one who has reached it. "The gods beginning with Prajāpati": those headed by the four-faced Brahmā. "She spoke" (*prāha*): she said what is about to be told. Regarding the word *āha*, Śākaṭāyana states: "'Āha' is an indeclinable that resembles a case ending, used in the sense of 'said'. In this context, there is a compound according to *Pāṇini* 2.2.18 (*kugatiprādayaḥ*).
Therefore, since this is the form of the root *brū-* in the present tense (*laṭ*), there is no requirement for the word *sma*. (37)
O gods, it is known to you that Viṣṇu, in his universal form, has placed this exceedingly great burden upon those who are virtuous in their conduct. (38)

"It is known": O gods, that which is known by you—that is understood by you—is as follows: by Viṣṇu, who possesses a universal form (viśvarūpa), a most heavy burden (mahīyān bhāraḥ)—a burden greater than the burdens of mountains and the like—has been placed upon those of virtuous character (dharmaśīla), those whose nature is righteousness, and the righteous. The phrase "that it has been placed" is connected with the preceding clause "it is known by you. Because the relative pronoun *yat* occurs in the subsequent sentence, the demonstrative pronoun *tat* is not used in the preceding sentence.

In the phrase "yat tat," the word *tat* (that) does not function as a correlative reference to the word *yat* (which). Rather, it refers to a well-known fact, such as in the verse: "The earth is supported by seven [classes]: by cows, Brahmins, the Vedas, chaste women, speakers of truth, donors, and those of virtuous character. This is because there is a rule that a word *tat* situated in proximity to a word *yat* must, by entering into the category of restatement (*anuvāda*), refer to something already established. As it has been stated in the *Kāvyaprakāśikā*:

“The word *tat* (that), standing in proximity to the word *yat* (which), refers to what is well-known. In the word *viditam* (known), the suffix *kta* is applied while the rule “*matibuddhipūjārthebhyaś ca*” [Pāṇini 3.2.188] is in force. By the connection with that [suffix], according to the rule “*ktasya ca vartamāne*” [Pāṇini 2.3.67], the genitive case is used in *bhavatām* (of you). In the word *mahattaram*, the suffix *īyasun* is added to the word *mahat* (great) according to the rule “*dvivacanavibhajyopapade tarab-īyasunau*” [Pāṇini 5.3.57].

Although no specific word to be compared (*upapada*) is explicitly mentioned here, nevertheless, the suffix occurs when there is a desire to express excellence with reference to a correlative (*pratiyogin*) present in the mind; for Vāmana has stated: "The superlative suffixes (*ātiśāyinika*) occur even when the correlative is mental" (Kāvyālaṅkārasūtra 5.2.60). || 38 ||
Another reading: "It is known to you that by Viṣṇu, in his universal form, a great burden has been placed upon those whose nature is righteousness."
Now, we are being trampled by countless, wondrous, and lofty mountains of Rākṣasas, who are devoted to unrighteousness and destroyers of the bridge of dharma. (39)

"Adharma" means now, at this time. "By those devoted to unrighteousness" (adharmanighnaiḥ) means those dependent on or impelled by unrighteousness. For this very reason, "by those who break the bridge of dharma" (dharmasetuvibhedakaiḥ) means those who shatter the boundaries of righteousness. "Innumerable" (asaṃkhyaiḥ) means devoid of number, or lacking in battle because there is no opposition; for the *Ratnamālā* states: "The word *saṃkhyā* refers to unity and so forth, while *saṃkhya* refers to battle. "Exalted" (tuṅgaiḥ) means elevated by valor. "Marvelous" (adbhutaiḥ) means wonderful.

"By the Rākṣasa-mountains; I am being trampled. This is the present tense (laṭ), third person singular, in the passive voice of the root *kram*. Although there is a prohibition against a genitive compound in the phrase "by those who break the bridge of Dharma" (*dharmasetuvibhedakaiḥ*) according to the rule *kartari ca* (Pāṇini 2.2.16), nevertheless, some justify such usage on the grounds that the group beginning with *yājaka* is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class). Others, however, maintain that the prohibition of compounding applies specifically to the genitive case characterized by its connection with a *kṛt*-suffix, and thus they establish the compound by means of the "residual" genitive (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*).
The author of the commentary named Sunītikīrti states that the commencement of the section prohibiting the sixth-case (genitive) compound pertains to the subject of accentuation.
Another reading: "Now I am being overwhelmed by countless, lofty mountains of asuras, who are devoted to unrighteousness and are destroyers of the bridge of dharma."

"Therefore, by the hosts of gods who have contemplated the welfare of the world, let that be done so that I may neither fall nor be split apart. (40) Regarding "therefore" (*ataḥ*): for this reason. By the "hosts of gods" (*suragaṇaiḥ*) who have "contemplated the welfare of the world" (*ālocitajagaddhitaiḥ*), meaning those who have considered the benefit of the people—let it be done in such a way that I do not fall due to excessive weight, and that I am not split, nor do I become broken of my own accord. The suffix *yak* is used here in the sense of the reflexive object (*karmakartari*). The verb form is in the imperative (*loṭ*) to express a request. (40)
Another reading: "Therefore, together with the hosts of gods who have deliberated upon the welfare of the world, act in such a way that I neither fall nor am split apart."
Thus, having been dispatched with this mission by the Earth, those dwellers of heaven understood that it was indeed the beloved of her Lord alone who was capable of bearing that burden. (41)

"Thus" (iti) means by the earth, the supporter of beings. "In this manner" (iti) refers to the way already described. "Those entrusted with the mission" (nisṛṣṭārthāḥ) means those to whom the task has been assigned or whose purpose has been communicated. "Those dwellers of heaven" (divaukasaḥ) are the gods. "Of him who was dear to her" (tatpriyasya) means of Nārāyaṇa himself, who was dear to that earth. "The removal of her burden" (tadbhāraharaṇam). "They knew it to be possible" (kṣamam) means they considered it feasible. They "thought" (aviduḥ); the root *vid* is used in the sense of "knowing" (according to Dhātupāṭha 2.59), and here it takes the present tense suffix (*laṭ*). The substitution of *jus* for *jhi* occurs according to Pāṇini 3.4.109: *sijabhyastavidibhyaś ca*. || 41 ||
Placing the Mother of the World at their head, they went far ahead of even the mind and, having approached the God who reclines upon the ocean of milk, praised him with hymns.

"Placing before them," etc. O gods, having placed the Earth, the sustainer of the world, before them; even surpassing the mind (*manas*)—that is, even more swift than the mental faculty—they went a great distance, reaching as far as the northern shore of the Ocean of Milk. There they praised the Lord Puruṣottama, who reclines upon the Ocean of Milk, extolling him from all sides in various ways. (42)
Salutations to you, who shine in the midst of the three Vedas, who possess the three abodes, who have five causes, the bestower of boons, and the consumer of both external and internal oblations.

"Trivedī": the collection of the three Vedas is the *trivedī*; to him who shines (*dīptāya*) within that, manifesting as the object to be propounded. By the rule "matibuddhipūjārthebhyaś ca" (Pāṇini 3.2.188), the suffix *kta* is applied in the sense of the present tense due to the word "ca. "Pañcahetaye": to him whose five weapons (*hetayaḥ*)—namely the conch, discus, mace, sword, and the Śārṅga bow—are his instruments. "Varadāya": to the giver of boons, who bestows upon his devotees whatever they desire.

Salutations to You, the consumer of both external and internal oblations; thus You are described. "External oblation" refers to the sacrificial offerings such as *caru*, *puroḍāśa*, and *sānnāyya*; "internal" refers to the substance of the oblation in the sacrifice called *prapadana*, which is the life-force (*jīva*) itself. To You who consume both of these—to the Three-Aboded One (*Tridhāman*), the Supreme Person (*Puruṣottama*)—be homage. The term "Three-Aboded" (*Tridhāman*) refers to the Blessed Lord, for He possesses three abodes (*dhāman*): the forms of the Ocean of Milk, the Solar Orb, and the Supreme Abode (*paramapada*).

The *Vaijayantī* states: “*Tridhāman* refers to Keśava and Agni. Consequently, by the term *tridhāman*, Agni is understood; thereafter follow the qualifying attributes intended to distinguish him. For he shines in the center of the northern *uttaravedi* during the animal and soma sacrifices. He is also the one with seven weapons (*saptaheti*), as there is scriptural mention of a sevenfold flame in passages such as: “Kālī, Karālī, Manojava,” and so forth.

"‘The flame of the sun, a weapon, a blaze of fire, and missiles’—thus says Amara. Furthermore, there is the phrase ‘possessing glory alone,’ based on the Smṛti: ‘One should desire glory from the consumer of oblations (fire). And he consumes only external sacrificial offerings.

Thus, although the subject (*viśeṣya*) refers to Puruṣottama (the Supreme Person), since it is applied to the irrelevant fire by virtue of the context, its distinction from that [fire] is manifested through the power of the qualifiers (*viśeṣaṇa*). Therefore, this is a suggestion (*dhvani*) of the figure of speech ‘Distinction’ (*vyatireka*), rooted in the power of the words. [43]
Your greatness is not dependent on another; the splendor of others is under Your own control;
Your pastimes are governed by compassion—protect us who have bowed before You. 44.

Regarding the word *ananyā*: "dependent on another" (*anyādhīna*) means dependent upon someone else; here the locative case is used in the sense of a sphere of influence (*vaiṣayika-adhikaraṇa*). The compound is formed by the rule of splitting the *yoga* (i.e., *saptamī* can stand independently). Amara states: “*Adhīna*, *nighna*, and *āyatta* [mean dependent]. Alternatively, in the analysis *anyasmin svāmini adhi* ("subordinate to another master"), the compound is formed by the rule *saptamī śauṇḍaiḥ* (Pāṇini 2.1.40), because the word *adhi* is included among the *śauṇḍa*-type words.

Because it is a compound with *adhi* as the final member, the suffix *kha* is applied in its own sense (*svārthe*) according to the rule: “The suffix *kha* occurs after *aṣaḍakṣa*, *āśitaṅgu*, *alaṅkarma*, and *alam-puruṣa* when they have *adhi* as their final member” (Pāṇini 5.4.7). Thus, the meaning is that he is dependent on both ways. This same explanation applies to the words *svādhīna* and so forth as well. He is *ananyādhīna* because he is not dependent on another; such is his majesty. His sovereignty (*vaibhava*) surpasses that of others, such as Brahmā and the rest, who are themselves dependent.

O You whose activity—consisting of the slaying of Rāvaṇa and other such deeds—is dependent upon compassion; being thus endowed, protect us who are prostrate before You, guarding us on all sides. It is said "dependent upon compassion" because one who is merciless does not protect even those who are prostrate. Regarding the Lord's prayer for the protection of the world through the restraint of the whip and other punishments, the epithet "dependent upon [Your own will]" contains a reason: even if the restraint of the whip and so forth is carried out by others, it must be performed with regard for the power obtained through Your grace.

Therefore, setting aside the begging of alms from others, the intention is that you alone are to be petitioned, and no one else, according to the principle: "Or rather, because they are equal [in status], it may be after one day" (MS 8.3.11). If even the glory of the Blessed One were dependent on another, then by that same logic he alone would be the one to be petitioned; but since that is not the case, it is said with this underlying thought: "not dependent on another" (ananyādhīna). || 44 ||
You, who shine with floods of the jewels of virtue and are an ocean of compassion, perform a dance through the splendor of your emanations, as if through waves.

"Sa" refers to You. "Guṇas" are qualities such as knowledge (*jñāna*), power (*śakti*), strength (*bala*), sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), and so forth; these are the "jewels" (*ratna*). By their "floods" (*ogha*), meaning by their multitudes, You are "blazing," that is, manifesting. You are an "ocean of compassion" (*dayāmbudhi*), like a sea that is a vast receptacle for mercy, or one whose very form is the ocean. You are "Bhagavān. By means of "manifestations and incarnations" (*vyūhavibhavaiḥ*): the "manifestations" (*vyūha*) are Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha; the "incarnations" (*vibhava*) are the descents such as Raghunātha and others. By these, You perform a "tāṇḍava dance"—that is, a dramatic performance—just as waves and ripples do upon the sea.

In the case of the ocean, however, it means "leaping up. It "spreads" (tanoti). By the use of the word *bhavat*, since there is an absence even of the underlying base (*sthānin*) for the proximate pronoun *yuṣmad*, the first person is indicated according to the rule *śeṣe prathamaḥ* [Pāṇini 1.4.108]. Through this, it is suggested that the Compassionate One’s assumption of incarnations and so forth for the protection of devotees is natural; thus, it is implied that he must descend even now for the sake of protection. || 45 ||
Who is able to define you, who are unknowable even by the Vedas—which, though initially revealed solely through you, subsequently refer to none other than you? 46.

Regarding the phrase *tvadeka*: "In the beginning" means at the start of the great creation (*mahāsarga*). The compound *tvadekavyañjitaiḥ* is analyzed as follows: *ekavyañjitāḥ* means "manifested by one"; then, following the pattern of the *Śivabhāgavata*, it is a compound meaning "manifested by you alone" (*tvayā ekavyañjitāḥ*). Otherwise, if the words *tvad* and *eka* were first compounded, the word *eka* would have been placed first according to the rule *pūrvakāla-eka-sarva-jarat-purāṇa-* etc., which prescribes that *eka* precedes in such compounds. It is the established principle of the scriptures (*śāstramaryādā*) that at the beginning of the great creation, the Vedas—characterized by the same sequential order as they had operated in each preceding Kalpa—are manifested by the Lord in that very same way.

In those other than you; by those "not having this as their primary aim"—that is, those for whom "this" (the manifest world) is not the primary object to be established as the principal subject; meaning, those whose final purport does not terminate in anything distinct from you. According to the *Ratnamālā*: “*Pura* [is used] in the senses of 'distant,' 'other,' and 'principal'. By such *nigamas*, i.e., the Vedas. You—who are "unapproachable," meaning indefinable—who is able to delimit you? Who is capable of defining you?

The *Ratnamālā* states: "The word *nigama* refers to certainty, a city, a path, the Veda, and the merchant's road. To suggest that if even this [reality], though expounded by such vast masses of the Vedas whose sole purport is that one thing, cannot be correctly determined, then what need is there to mention that another person cannot determine it—this is expressed by the phrase "by those other than you who do not have this as their purport."

If there were some other speaker of the Vedas, then, due to the possibility of defects in that speaker, their lack of capacity for definitive determination would be established by that very fact and not from the weightiness of the subject matter; having raised this doubt, it was said: "manifested by you alone" (tvadekavyañjitaiḥ). || 36 ||
For those who desire to reach the further shore of your immeasurable greatness, the goal that serves as their evening rest-house for the travelers on the path of the Vedas becomes futile. 47.

He elaborates upon the very fact that [the Lord] cannot be reached even by the *nigamas* (scriptural texts): "Of the immeasurable," etc. "Immeasurable" means unlimited. "Of that greatness" means of Your majesty. "The further shore" means the limit. "Of those desiring to go" refers to those wishing to reach it. "The Vedas themselves are travelers" means they are constant wayfarers. The suffix *ṇa* is applied according to the rule *pantho ṇa nityam* [Pāṇini 5.1.76], and there is the substitution of the word *panthā*. For them, "the path where the evening home is"—that is, that path where the very time of evening serves as their dwelling—such a destination is "vitathā," meaning futile or vain.

Just as men who have set out to reach a place that cannot be attained even in a full human lifetime might travel every day until evening yet never reach that destination; so too, the Vedas, having begun to describe Your majesty—which transcends the range of speech and mind—though they describe it in every possible way through the domain of words, are not capable of describing it in its entirety. This is the meaning. The poetic figure is *rūpaka* (metaphor). || 48 ||

How can your play with those who bow down to you—who are yourself bowed to by others—be described, O Giver of Boons, by anyone, as you sport with those lowly beings who seek boons from you, just as a father sports with his sons? (48)

"Of him who is to be bowed to" means of him who is to be saluted by all the worlds. "Even the lowly"—that is, even the minor ones such as Indra and others—"bow down" through incarnations such as Upendra. "The giver of boons" means the bestower of boons upon all the worlds. "Nevertheless," [even] among Brahmā and the others, there are those seeking boons. "With sons" such as Kāśyapa and others, he is "possessed of fathers. How, in what manner, has your play (*krīḍā*) proceeded? Or by which person is it described? Your mode of play is inconceivable;
therefore, the meaning is that no one at all is capable of describing you. (48)
O Lord, playing like an actor through various distinct roles, you nourish the wondrous aesthetic flavor (rasa) for those men who possess undivided devotion. 49.

"Like an actor" (*naṭavat*): O Lord, "like an actor" means equal to an actor. The suffix *vati* is applied according to the rule: *“When there is equality with that, if it is an action, the suffix -vat- is used”* [Pāṇini 5.1.115]. By various roles (*bhūmikā*), meaning by the different manifestations such as the Fish, the Tortoise, and so forth. The *Viśva* lexicon states: *“The word *bhūmikā* may refer to a composition or to the assumption of another form.”* The *Vaijayantī* states: *“The costume for each [role] is called a *bhūmikā*.”* *Dīvyan* means playing or sporting.

O You, You nourish—that is, You manifest—the wondrous *rasa* (the bliss of liberation), which has never been experienced before and is thus a marvel within *saṃsāra*, for those of single-minded devotion (*ekāntin*) whose nature is such that there exists no other object of focus for them. The meaning is: You unite those who are intent on contemplating the secrets of Your incarnations with the granting of liberation. The sense is that just as an actor nourishes the *rasa* called "wonder" in the audience—whose hearts are focused on nothing else—by means of various costumes representing characters such as Rāma and others, so it is here. This is the figure of speech known as *upamā* (simile). 49.
For all things possessing diverse sprouts from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, water is merely your play, for those whose roots are karma. (50)

"Beginning with Brahmā": those for whom Brahmā is the first—the initial stalk—and the grasses and so forth are the final limit, they are "all living beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass. These alone are the various sprouts belonging to those who possess them, that is, those who partake of them. Of the "kanda-roots of karma"—where *karman* itself is the *kanda*, the root of the crop—it is solely Your play that is the water.

The meaning is that the roots of karma, aided by the sprinkling of water which is merely the form of Your play, produce sprouts in the form of the manifold phenomenal world (*prapañca*). Here, because the superimposition of "water-ness" upon the Lord’s play serves the purpose of the contextual effect—namely, the production of the sprouts of the phenomenal world—the figure of speech is *pariṇāma* (transformation). || 50 ||
Your qualities are peerless and unsurpassed, for You possess Your own inherent stability without support, are the sovereign without limiting adjuncts, and are the independent ruler. (51)

"Without support" (*nirādhāra*) means that which has its own inherent stability (*sthemā*), being independent of any external support. It refers to the one who is the Lord without limiting adjuncts (*nirupādhika-śeṣin*), who by his very nature is the primary cause of the entire universe. "Independent" (*nirapekṣa*) means acting without dependence on any other auxiliary causes; such is the Controller, the regulator of the world. Those qualities of His are "without equal or superior," meaning devoid of anything equal to or greater than them.

In the world, indeed, the stability of stable things such as mountains is dependent upon a support; the status of kings as the superiors (śeṣin) toward their servants and so forth is conditioned by adventitious factors such as the payment of wages; and their very exercise of control over the kingdom and so forth is dependent upon ministers and others. But for the Blessed One, stability and other such qualities are not of this nature. Thus, the poetic figure of contrast (vyatireka)—consisting in their superiority over the stability of mountains and the like—is suggested.

And that [suggestion], being manifested, is an auxiliary factor for the establishment of the expressed meaning—which consists in its being unsurpassed and superior; thus, it is a variety of *guṇībhūtavyaṅgya* (subordinate suggestion) named *vācyasiddhyaṅga* (auxiliary to the establishment of the expressed). From the word *sthira*, the suffix *iman* is applied according to the rule *“varṇadṛḍhādibhyaḥ ṣyac ca”* (*Pāṇini* 5.1.123), where the *ca* implies the inclusion of *iman*. Then, by the rule *“priyasthira...”* (*Pāṇini* 6.4.157), the word *sthira* undergoes the substitution of *stha*, and by the rule *“prakṛtyaikāc”* (*Pāṇini* 6.4.163), the original form is retained; thus, the form *sthemā* is produced. || 51 ||
Shining within those of unclouded intellect like a wish-fulfilling gem, you grant every desired object, for your radiance cannot be obstructed.

"Untroubled" (*anāvila*) means that your splendor is not to be set aside; its radiance cannot be overcome by other lights. You, shining within—the heart—of those with untroubled intellects, meaning those whose minds are not clouded by activities opposed to contemplation, grant everything desired once you have been made the object of uninterrupted reflection.

The meaning is that, having liberated those from the worlds of transmigration, you grant everything they desire by mere volition (saṃkalpa), according to the process described in the scriptural passages concerning the liberated, such as: "If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers, by his mere volition the fathers arise" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.2.1). You are like a wish-fulfilling gem (cintāmaṇi); for that too, by virtue of being a divine jewel, possesses a radiance that cannot be eclipsed by other lights, and when thought of, it bestows the desired object. || 52 ||
For the embodied being exhausted in the desert wilderness of saṃsāra, immersion in the nectar-stream of devotion to you has been prescribed. (53)

Regarding the word *saṃsāre*: *saṃsāra* itself is a desert (*maru*), a waterless region, because it is devoid of pleasure and thus sapless. Its wilderness (*kāntāra*) is a difficult path; for those who perform sacrifices and works of public utility, it takes the form of the paths of smoke and so forth, which serve as the means for coming and going between this world and the next. For sinners, it is the miserable, difficult state of the third place. As Amarasimha states: "A wilderness (*kāntāra*) is a difficult path" (AK 2.1.36). In that [wilderness], for one who is exhausted—meaning weary from the coming and going—and for an embodied being (*dehin*).

Devotion to You alone is a river of nectar, a stream of ambrosia; immersion in that [river] is "prescribed," meaning it is taught as removing the fatigue of coming and going, as in passages such as: "But by unswerving devotion, O Arjuna, I—who am of such a nature—can be known in truth, seen in truth, and entered into, O scorcher of the foe" (BhG 11.54). Here, because the superimposition of the quality of being a "river of nectar" upon devotion serves the purpose of removing the fatigue of the path of saṃsāra, there is the figure of speech *pariṇāma* (transformation). || 53 ||
For me, who am suffering and reeling within the whirlpool of the ocean of calamities,
you— endowed with every excellence— are the great raft that delivers one across.

Regarding the word *durita*: *durita* itself is the ocean (*udanvān*); in its whirlpool (*āvarta*), that is, the swirling of the waters. Amarasimha states: “*Āvarta* is the whirling of waters” (AK 1.10.528). By metaphorical usage, *āvarta* here refers to the ripening of evil deeds (*duritaparipāka*). In that state, for one who is reeling—that is, wandering about; suffering and being afflicted. The suffix *yak* is applied to the root *duḥkh* because it is listed among the *kaṇḍvādi* group. The sense is: "for the embodied being who has come for refuge."

"Complete" means unbroken; "qualities" refers specifically to qualities such as the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*). He is "endowed with" or enriched by these, which are like "threads" (*sūtra*). You alone are the "great raft"—this is a *vyasta-rūpaka* (distributive metaphor). You are the "savior," the one who delivers others across [the ocean of existence]. The distinction here is that while in the previous verse devotion was stated to be the means to liberation, here it is surrender (*prapatti*). As before, the poetic figure is *pariṇāma* (transformation/metaphorical identification). || 54 ||
Since you cannot be delimited by space, time, and so forth, you alone are the illustration [of your own nature], for everything other than you is excluded from it. (55)

"Of that which is not delimited" means: by space, time, and so forth; by space because of omnipresence (*vibhutva*), by time because of eternity (*nityatva*), and by substance because of being the self of all (*sarvātmakatva*). "Of yours" means: you alone are [that]. "Illustration" (*nidarśana*) means an example (*dṛṣṭānta*). "Other than you"—namely, the sky and so forth, which are well-known for their pervasiveness and other qualities. "By way of negative concomitance" (*vyatirekataḥ*): the term "illustration" is to be supplied. The meaning is that, in the sequence beginning with "like the sky and so forth, it is not delimited by space," there is a negative example (*vyatireka-dṛṣṭānta*).

In this regard, "you alone are the illustration" constitutes the figure *ananvaya* (non-comparison), because there is a relationship between the standard of comparison and the object of comparison for that very same single entity. Furthermore, "distinct from you" constitutes the figure *vyatireka* (distinction), because of the description of the Blessed One’s superiority over the sky and other such things. Since these two figures mutually nourish one another, there is a *saṃkara* (commixture) of them. || 55 ||
Capable of undoing everything, doing everything, or even doing otherwise at will—
such a mere fragment of power as that is yours, O Lord, whose companion is your own resolve.

"To not create" means the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*). "At the proper time" means at the specific occasion appropriate for each [action]. "To not create, to create, and even to create otherwise": this refers to not creating during the periods of dissolution (*pralaya*), creating during the beginnings of creation (*sarga*) and so forth, and creating otherwise by successively displacing the authority of former Indras and others during the various *manvantaras* and establishing other Indras in their stead. "Having you as his companion in resolve" (*saṅkalpasacivaḥ*) means having your resolve as his assistant; the *Vaijayantī* lexicon states: "The words *sahāya* and *saciva* [mean 'companion']."

"Your fragment of power" means having the form of a fragment of Your power; that is Time itself. "Adequate" (alam) means sufficient. A mere fragment of Your power is sufficient for the activity of the universe. The sense is: how can Your complete power be perceived? In passages such as, "Therefore, that portion of Hari which is said to be of the nature of Time," the fact that Time is a fragment of the Lord's power is well-established. || 56 ||

Another reading: *akartum akhilaṃ kartum* → "That which is studied as the root of all that is to be undone and all that is to be done, and that which is the rootless source of all effects—that you are the target of yogas, characterized by the Lakṣmī-kaustubha gem. (57)

"That which has a root" refers to the entire universe beginning with space (*viyat*), which is an effect. "That which has no root" is that which is without cause. It is studied in the Upaniṣads, such as in the passage: "And for this, there is no progenitor, nor is there any lord" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.9). That [Brahman], characterized by Lakṣmī and the Kaustubha—the gem named Kaustubha being its mark—is You, the Supreme Brahman, who are the goal and the intended object of the *yogas*, namely the higher knowledges (*paravidyā*) such as the meditation on the *dahara* (the small space within the heart). || 57 ||
For those striving to attain either the threefold aims of life or liberation,
your grace is the guarantor of long life even through the cosmic dissolutions.

Regarding the term *trivargam*: it is the group (*varga*) of the three, namely virtue (*dharma*), wealth (*artha*), and pleasure (*kāma*). As Amarasimha states: "The *trivarga* consists of virtue, pleasure, and wealth" (AK 2.6.931). Or else, it refers to *apavarga*, which is liberation (*mokṣa*). *Pratilabdhum* means to obtain or attain. *Prayasyatām* means of those who are striving or making effort. *Tvadanugrahaḥ* is your favor or grace. *Pralayeṣv api*: even during the cosmic dissolutions. *Dīrghāyuḥ*: long-lived. *Pratibhūḥ*: a guarantor or surety (*lagnaka*).

Just as those who live by usury lend money for the sake of interest, trusting in a guarantor, so too do the virtuous perform actions for the sake of the three goals (trivarga) and liberation (apavarga), trusting that Your grace alone will yield fruit even in other kalpas. The sense is that the presiding deities of specific rites, such as Agni, cannot exist in other kalpas. Since the superimposition of the status of a guarantor upon the Lord’s grace serves the purpose of the current subject matter—which is the exertion [of religious duty]—this constitutes the poetic figure *pariṇāma* (transformation). || 58 ||
That which is the single syllable Brahman, endowed with all the Vedas, the savior of all living beings—that is You, and it is Your designator. (59)

"That which is one": that which is endowed with all sacred traditions (*āmnāya*), being present at the beginning and end of all the Vedas, according to the Smṛti: "One should always place the *praṇava* of Brahman at the beginning and at the end" (Mānava Dharma Śāstra 2.74). It is the savior (*tāraka*) for all living beings, serving as the means for crossing the ocean of worldly existence. That which is the one imperishable Brahman, the single-syllabled Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*)—well known from the text: "'Om' is the single-syllabled Brahman" (Bhagavad Gītā 8.13)—that is You; that belongs to You.

The meaning is this: You alone are that Supreme Brahman, which is described as the signifier (*vācaka*) and the signified (*abhidheya*), as in “*Oṃ* is Brahman,” and “*Oṃ*, *tat*, *sat*: this is declared to be the threefold designation of Brahman” (Bhagavad Gītā 17.23), and so forth—being both the form of the *praṇava* and that which is signified by the *praṇava*. || 59 ||
Another reading: *tat tvaṃ* → *tvaṃ tat*:
"For those virtuous ones who emerge from existence with their hands grasped by you, there is no hand to support them as they sink, for the multitude of evils. (60)

"By you": for those who have grasped your hand—that is, whose hands have been taken hold of for the sake of their deliverance. Therefore, "from existence," that is, from the well of *saṃsāra*. "Of those emerging": of the virtuous knowers of Brahman. For the Śruti says: "If one knows that 'Brahman exists,' then they know him as truly existing" (TU 2.6.1). "Of those sinking": of the multitude of sins, the mass of evil. "There is no support for the hand. Therefore, the meaning is that there is no emergence together with them.

The *Viśvaprakāśa* states: “*Jāta* [means] both birth and a collection. According to the manner stated in the passage, “In the same way, the fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes” (Bhagavad Gītā 4.37), the immersion of the collection of sins is mentioned with the intention that they are destroyed by knowledge; and according to the manner stated in the passage, “He shakes off his good and evil deeds... his beloved kinsmen enjoy his good deeds, while those who are not beloved enjoy his evil deeds” (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.4), it is mentioned with the intention that they are transferred elsewhere.

By this it is indicated that for those who have reached the Blessed One, there is no returning again—just as there is none for those who have reached the state of Brahmā and others—because of the absence of karma, which is the seed of saṃsāra. || 60 ||
{1}: I have the following reading: "He shakes off his good and evil deeds; his dear kinsmen take up his good deeds, and those who are not dear take up his evil deeds.
Those who observe the vow of the *cātaka* bird—protecting nothing else—cling to you, who practice the meditation on supportlessness. (61)

"Ananya" means those who are single-mindedly devoted; their very protection is their vow, and he who possesses that is "ananyarakṣāvratī. Just as in the case of *sarvadhanī* or *sarvakeśī*, the possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) is appropriately applied even after a *karmadhāraya* compound. To you, such as you are—those who practice the vow of the *cātaka* bird. The *cātaka* birds are those creatures single-mindedly devoted to the cloud; they are so called because it is their habit to practice that vow of exclusive devotion. Thus, they are those who are restricted solely to you.

"Nirālambanabhāvanam" means that in which there is a meditation—a mental activity—without support; that is to say, one devoid of support for other means such as the yoga of devotion (bhaktiyoga). It means, in short, being free from hope for other means. They "take hold of" or "resort to" [the Lord]. Since this state of "having nothing" (akiñcanya), characterized by the absence of hope for other means, is a qualification of the person entitled to resort [to the Lord], it is described as "meditation without support. || 61 ||
For those who have never before slept, you, whose light never sets,
bring about for men a waking from which there is no further sleep.

"Anidam" means those for whom this transmigratory existence (*saṃsṛti*), which is sleep, has proceeded from time immemorial and is not preceded by anything else—those persons. You are the sun that never sets; you bring about liberation, which is a waking state from which there is no returning to sleep. Just as the rising sun awakens those who are asleep, so too, shining within the heart, you release those caught in the cycle of worldly existence—this is the meaning.

Here, there is a *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) in that the concealment and manifestation of the soul's true nature in saṃsāra and apavarga are determined through the states of sleep and waking. There is a *pariṇāma* (transformation) because the superimposition of "sun-ness" upon the Lord serves the purpose of the contextual effect, namely the induction of waking. Furthermore, the qualification "not setting" (*anastamayatva*) is the cause for the absence of further sleep following the sun's setting; thus, there is a *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic figure of causal indication) based on the meaning of the words. Consequently, these figures are combined in a *saṅkara* (commixture).
And by that, the distinction from the well-known Bhānumat is manifested; thus, there is the suggestion of a figure of speech (alaṅkāradhvani) through a figure of speech (alaṅkāreṇa). || 62 ||

"You are the life of those who have come to you for refuge; you alone are the protector of us whose sole shelter is you. Quickly dispel our calamity, as the sun dispels the darkness. Regarding "tvadeka-": You are the "life of those who have come for refuge" (*śaraṇāgata-jīvana*), meaning the savior. You are the one for those of whom you are the "sole shelter" (*eka-śaraṇa*), that is, the sole protector. "Of us" (*naḥ*) means of ourselves. According to Amarasimha, "shelter" (*śaraṇa*) refers to both a house and a protector. "Calamity" (*vipad*); "darkness" (*tamisrā*) means gloom. Like the "sun" (*bhāskara*), "quickly" (*kṣipram*) means swiftly; "dispel" (*kṣipa*) means cast away.
"Furthermore, *dhvānta* and *tamisra* [denote] darkness; *tamisrā* [denotes] night and the two types of blindness," according to the *Amaraśeṣa*. (63)

Another reading: *naḥ kṣipa kṣipraṃ tamisrām iva* → "Cast away our darkness quickly, as if the sun were rising while the sun already exists; like demons who arise as counter-suns for the affliction of the world, destroy them with your own splendor. (64)

"Satīti" means: while the Sun is present (satī), those who rise up like counter-suns—namely the Asuras in the form of Kaṃsa and others—are born for the affliction of the worlds; that is, they become sources of calamity. Even counter-suns cause distress because they are portents of ill omen. [Destroy them] by your own splendor and power; in the case of the Sun, [by his] light. "Jahi" means destroy or annihilate. The substitution of *ja* for the root *han* is according to the rule: *hanter jaḥ* [Pāṇini 6.4.36]. || 64 ||
Thus praised by the gods who desired the destruction of the Daitya, he, who was invisible to others, suddenly granted his vision out of compassion. (65)

"He" refers to the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). "The slaughter of the Daityas" means the killing of the Asuras; the suffix *kyap* with the substitution of *t* for *han* is applied in the sense of the action according to Pāṇini 3.3.108 (*hanasta ca*). By the gods who desired that [slaughter], he was thus praised in the manner described. He is visible to those who are non-dual and single-mindedly devoted. Suddenly—that is, unexpectedly—as Amara states: "But 'sahasā' is used for the unexpected. Out of compassion, he gave them his vision;
the meaning is that he manifested himself before them. || 65 ||
Another reading: *dayayā darśanam* → *darśanam dayayā*.
Then the gods beheld him seated upon the couch of Śeṣa, appearing like a cloud that had mounted an autumnal cloud, as if he were something altogether different. (66)

Regarding the word *tataḥ*: it means "thereafter," immediately following His manifestation. "The gods" refers to Brahmā and the others. *Śeṣa* is the couch or bed; [they saw Him] seated upon that. The verb *tiṣṭhati* (to stand/be) becomes transitive through the change in its prefix. For this very reason, [the text says] "He who had ascended the autumnal clouds. [They saw Him] as something different, extraordinary, and transcendent—standing like a cloud, a water-bearer. They beheld Him. Here, there is a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) in the form of a supposition. || 66 ||
Seated together with his wife, who was marked by the signs of a lotus,
who possessed a physical form according to her own will, and who indicated the perfection of his sovereign power.

"Patnyā" means with his wife, who was seated together with him upon the entire couch (*śeṣaparyaṅke*). The suffix *kvasu* is used here according to Pāṇini 3.2.108 (*sadavasaśruvaḥ*). She was characterized by the lotus itself as her mark—that is, she was visible with a lotus in her hand (*padmahastayā*). "Svecchayā" means by her own will alone, without being subject to the power of karma. "Śarīriṇyā" refers to the embodied Śrī Mahālakṣmī. He is one whose abundance of sovereignty—the excellence of his supreme majesty—is indicated by her.

From this point onward, the connection of these seven verses is with the preceding word "they saw. Since it is heard in the context of the Supreme Brahman that "Hrī and Lakṣmī are your two wives" (Taittirīya Āraṇyaka 3.13.2), the sense is that being the husband of Lakṣmī is a characteristic mark of the Supreme State. || 67 ||
It was adorned with ornaments that were soft to the touch, pleasant, and fragrant,
as if they were flowers produced from the garden of the virtues of his own body.

"Sukumārāṇi" means delicate and soft; "sukhasparśāni" means those whose touch is pleasant—that is, endowed with specific touches that provide pleasure at particular times. Regarding the word *sukha*, the *Śabdārṇava* states: "In the sense of a cause of pleasure, it is used for pleasure itself. "Sugandhīni" means those which possess a beautiful fragrance; the suffix *it* is applied here according to Pāṇini 5.4.135 (*gandhasyedutpūtisusurabhibhyaḥ*). The compound [of these adjectives with "garments"] is a descriptive determinative (*viśeṣaṇasamāsa*), following the analogy of the term *khañjakubja* ("lame and hunchbacked").

His own body is a garden and grove for the virtues; it is adorned with ornaments—divine jewels—that stand as if they were its flowers. This is an ornament of poetic fancy (utprekṣā) suggested by a metaphor (rūpaka). || 68 ||
With limbs of immeasurable beauty that adorned one another and captivated the eyes of the world, she appeared as if her very ornaments were fashioned from her own form.

"Ārañjita" means by those who have colored the eyes of the world—that is, by those who have made the eyes of people full of affection. "Anyonyaparikarmitaiḥ" means by those mutually adorned with one another; the suffix *itac* is applied to the word *parikarma* because it belongs to the *ākṛtigaṇa* beginning with *tāraka*. In both these qualifiers, the cause is "by those of immeasurable beauty"—that is, by those of immeasurable loveliness. "Aṅgaiḥ" means by their limbs; "anukalpitabhūṣaṇam" means ornaments rendered secondary or merely supplementary.

The sense is that even compared to the ornaments, it is the limbs themselves that bring about a mutually superior splendor. Amara states: "The primary [option] should be the first alternative (kalpa), but the secondary (anukalpa) is inferior to that. Here, the qualification of the limbs serves as the reason for the ornaments being considered secondary; thus, the poetic figure is *kāvyaliṅga* (poetic cause), where the meaning of the words functions as the cause. || 69 ||
Their enthusiasm for victory was aroused by weapons of faultless efficacy,
as if by their own innate virtues such as heroism, prowess, and power.

Regarding the word *uttejitaiḥ*: "by means of blameless efforts" means by means of unfailing exertions. Oh! There is a metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) of another fault in the word *agha*, which usually denotes suffering or calamity, applied here to that [effort] which is appropriate. "By means of valor, prowess, power, and so forth": *śaurya* is strength; *vikrama* is the application of valor toward its objects—according to the *Vaijayantī*, "prowess is the exercise of valor"; *śakti* is capability, and "and so forth" refers to those beginning with that. "Innate" means established by one's own nature.

The *Vaijayantī* lexicon states that "innate" (*sahaja*), "own" (*nija*), and "inherent" (*ājāna*) are synonyms for "nature. [He was] "as if by his own qualities," meaning as if by his personal attributes; "by weapons" refers to the Sudarśana discus and others. "With the enthusiasm for victory sharpened" means that his exertion toward conquering the Asuras had become intensified upon seeing those weapons. || 70 ||
Within the ocean of his own splendor, he possesses a perfectly formed body by his very nature; through his majesty, he has arisen like a great sapphire of manifold beauty.

"His own luster" (*svakānti*) means the ocean of his very luster; "within it" (*antaḥ*) means in its midst. "A body naturally perfected" (*svataḥsiddhasaṃhananaṃ*) means a form that has been produced by itself alone, without being dependent on karma and so forth. Amarasimha states: "The word *gātra* means *vapus* (body) or *saṃhanana* (structure)" [AK 2.5.670]. "By greatness" (*mahimnā*) means by majesty. The sense is that without the creation of some [divine agent], there would be a natural variety [of form]; for such beauty as this could not possibly arise through [ordinary] creation, given the resulting diversity of limbs, colors, and features.

"Uditaṃ" means arisen or emerged. "Mahānīlaṃ" refers to a great sapphire (*indranīla*), as if it were a particular kind of gemstone. The sense is that even such a stone is perfected within the midst of the ocean. This is the figure of speech *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy). According to the *Ratnaśāstra*: "Those produced in the mine of Siṃhala are known as 'mahānīlas'. (71)
With the vehicle of the Veda,
adorned with the bracelets of its remaining portions and smeared with the fragrance of his own feet, he granted the longing for battle.

"By means of the form of the Vedas" (śrutirūpeṇa): he who is adorned by the bracelet that is his tail (śeṣakaṅkaṇaśobhī); by him who is smeared with the fragrance of his own feet (svāṅghrisaurabhadigdhena), meaning defiled by the scent of the Lord’s feet transferred at the time of being carried; by means of the vehicle in the form of the Vedas (śrutirūpeṇa vāhena), namely Suparṇa—since there is a scriptural statement regarding his being composed of the Vedas, beginning with "Thou art Suparṇa, the Garuḍa; the Trivṛt-stoma is thy head" (Kauṣītaki Upaniṣad 14.11); [he is] one to whom the desire for battle has been granted (dattasaṃgrāmadohalam), meaning one whose longing for combat has been bestowed.

The meaning is that, simply by the sight of Garuḍa, he conceived a longing for battle with the Daityas. According to the *Amaraśeṣa*, “*dolahaṃ dohadaṃ chandaḥ*” is among the synonyms for desire (*icchā*). || 72 ||
He was signaled by the army commander, who was bowing with devotion and conveying his message through the movement and stillness of his own cane, as he was giving his assent through gestures.

Regarding the phrase *svavetreṇa*: by him who, through the movement—that is, the shaking—of his own staff held in his hand, [those] were to be rendered motionless, that is, made still, and led to the presence of the God; the meaning is that, in order to prevent those being led to the God’s presence from crowding one another in a scramble to report their respective business, he would make them motionless merely by the movement of his own staff, by virtue of his authoritative command. The reading *niḥspanda* is preferred, as there is no occasion for the substitution of *ṣ* for *s*.

And it has been stated by Vāmana: "In the word *niṣpanda*, the substitution of *pa* for *spa* is to be considered. By the commander of the army, Viṣvaksena, who was bowed down with devotion—that is, prostrate through his devotion—the purpose (*prayojana*) was announced or made known. This was done by means of gestures, that is, by signs of the eyebrows. To him who was assenting—that is, promising "I shall give"—the root *śru* preceded by *prati* signifies a promise to grant the object requested.

Here, because of the subtle description of the master’s inherent nature of acting as a staff-bearer in his presence and his inherent nature of promising to fulfill the requests presented to him, the figure of speech is *svabhāvokti* (description of natural character). || 73 ||
The inhabitants of heaven regarded that sun— the imperishable lord of the stars— as one who brings no misfortune,
as the shoreless ocean of nectar.
"Without decline"—the denizens of heaven thought of that Blessed One as the sun without setting, the inexhaustible moon, the lord of stars, and the shoreless ocean of nectar, free from any limit.

The meaning is that the gods, beholding the god’s surpassing splendor, his graciousness, his delectability through his exquisite beauty and his nature as supreme bliss, and reflecting upon his distinctions such as being eternally risen, eternally uniform, unlimited, and unchanging, concluded in this sequence that he was some other kind of sun, one devoid of setting, and so forth. Here, because a single entity is described in various forms by virtue of the power of multiple meanings, there is the poetic figure *ullekha* (multiple description). || 74 ||
Beholding the god whose outstretched hands were open in the gesture of granting fearlessness, and who smiled with a faultless welcome, the wise attained the true fruit of their vision. (75)

"Abhaya" means the gods. "Whose fingertips are noble and renowned for the Abhaya [gesture]"—the *Vaijayantī* lexicon states: "The word *udāra* means great or renowned. "Sinless" means opposed to sin; it removes all suffering merely by being seen. "Whose gentle smile is a welcome"—meaning a mild smile in the form of an inquiry after one's welfare. The *Śabdārṇava* states: "'Welcome' and 'well-being' are considered appropriate expressions of affection when addressing someone. Having beheld that God...

They obtained the fruit of their sight. Although there were many eyes, the dual number used in the word *dṛśoḥ* (of the two eyes) is intended to denote the genus (*jāti*), because things of this kind are generally characterized by duality. As Vāmana said: "The genus of breasts and the like is generally characterized by duality" [Kāvyālaṅkārasūtravṛtti 5.1.17]. || 75 ||

Another reading: *dṛśoḥ phalam* → "The inhabitants of heaven, having understood the matter, reported the fruit of their vision to him who had already known the truth, as a further expression of welcome to him by whom all the Daityas had been slain. (76)

"From him"—that is, from the celestial gods (*nākinaḥ*). "To the one by whom all the Daityas were slain," meaning to the one by whom the entire host of Daityas, headed by Kālanemi, had been destroyed. "To the one who knows the matter": since the Daityas, having been slain, have now arisen on earth and are causing harassment once again, he has understood for himself the purpose of their arrival; thus, it means "to him who knows the reason for his own coming. To that Puruṣottama, they made known the cause—the root—of their welcome arrival. The dative case is used here according to the rule *karmaṇā yam abhipraiti* (Pāṇini 1.4.32), where it should be understood that the word "action" (*kriyā*) must also be included [so that the dative can express the recipient of an action]. || 76 ||
Another reading: *svāgateḥ punaḥ* → "Then, O Svāgata, these Kṣatriyas, having become such, are agitating this earth—those demons who, O Lord, acted like moths in your splendor. (77)

"Those... O Lord, in Your *tejas*—where *tejas* means majesty, for Yādava states: "The word *tejas* is used for strength, majesty, luster, flame, semen, butter, fire, and dharma"—in that [majesty], those *danujas* (demons) acted like moths (*śalabhāyitam*). Having become these Kṣatriyas, they now agitate this earth, this *kṣamā*.

In the expression *śalabhāyitam*, there is a *saṃkara* (commingling) of two figures: a simile (*upamā*) based on the comparison, and a hyperbole (*atiśayokti*) consisting of an identification rooted in paronomasia (*śleṣa*). || 77 ||
Another reading: "O Lord, those demons who acted like moths in your splendor have now become Kṣatriyas and are agitating this earth."
This earth, the source of the four human goals which arises from her as its support, and the progenitor of offerings to gods and ancestors, is now being oppressed by the burden of the Daityas. (78)

"Of the four" means of the four human goals (puruṣārtha), beginning with dharma. "By whose resort" means by taking recourse to her. "Production" means origination. For, depending upon the earth, religious duties such as sacrifices are to be accomplished, since they pertain to human beings; likewise, wealth and pleasure, which have that [dharma] as their root, exist both in this world and the next; and even liberation is dependent upon that [earth], being contingent on knowledge, according to such scriptural passages as, "They desire to know [Brahman] through sacrifice and through giving" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.22).

Therefore, the intention is that even the four goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*) arise only by depending upon the earth. She is the "progenitor of *havya* and *kavya*": *havya* is food for the gods, and *kavya* is food for the ancestors; as Amarasimha states: “*Havya* and *kavya* are the foods pertaining to the gods and the ancestors” (Amara-kośa 2.6.859). She is the progenitor of these two, meaning the Earth is the milch-cow of all medicinal herbs. The suffix *kvip* is applied according to the rule “*satsūdviṣadruha-*” (Pāṇini 3.2.61). She is "by the weight of the Daityas" (*daityabhārataḥ*).

The suffix *tasi* is added according to the rule “*ādyādibhya upasaṃkhyānam*” [Vārttika on Pāṇini 5.4.44]. It is split (*dīryate*). The suffix *yak* is applied to the root *dṝ* (meaning "to tear") in the sense of the object-as-agent (*karmakartṛ*), or alternatively, the suffix *śyan* is applied because the *divādi* class has not yet concluded. Therefore, the intended meaning is that this [Śruti], which is beneficial for all human goals, must necessarily be protected in every respect. || 78 ||
Born from the pillow of the crown of all the Vedas, this [Earth] rests solely upon your lotus feet, its stability dependent entirely on you. (79)

Then they say: "Since she has arisen from your feet, she must be protected by you alone"—this is expressed in the verse beginning with *jātā*. From the lotus-feet of you, the source of all the Vedas (*nikhilavedānām*), which are the supreme limbs (*uttamāṅgānām*)—that is, the Upaniṣads—because they serve as her support (*upadhānataḥ*) insofar as she is to be propounded and relied upon; the suffix *tasi* is used here according to Pāṇini 5.4.45 (*apādāne cāhīyaruhoḥ*). This Goddess was born from that lotus-foot of yours; her maintenance depends solely on you, and the task of supporting her is entrusted entirely to you.

Here, because the lotus-feet of the Blessed One are described as serving as a pillow for the head of the Vedas, it is understood that the Vedas themselves are metaphorically described as a person whose existence is brought about by taking refuge in them; thus, there is the figure of speech known as *ekadeśavivarti-rūpaka* (partial metaphor). Furthermore, in the phrase "from your lotus-feet," there is a simile (*upamā*); therefore, there is a *saṃsṛṣṭi* (conjunction) of these two figures. || 79 ||
O Lord, if you do not hasten to remove this burden,
the oceans with their vast waves will submerge the earth.

"Yadi" means: O Lord, if you do not hasten—that is, if you delay—in the removal of the burden, namely the relieving of the earth's weight, then the oceans, with their vast waves or great billows, will inundate the earth; that is to say, they will drench it. The meaning is that when the earth is pressed down in its center by the weight, the waters of the oceans, flowing toward the low-lying areas, will submerge it. || 80 ||
With a mind governed by compassion, may you, like a helmsman, ensure that this great earth does not sink, as if it were a large ship in the water. (81)

"By compassion": with a mind governed by compassion, with a heart dependent on pity; by you. "Possessing a helmsman," meaning possessing a navigator—Amara states: "A *karṇadhāra* is a navigator. This earth is like a great ship. In the waters—that is, in the waters of the ocean—let it not sink; let it not become submerged. Regarding the rule *māṅi luṅ* (Pāṇini 3.3.175), since this word *mā* is distinct from the *māṅ* root used in that rule and functions solely as a particle of prohibition, the use of the imperative (*loṭ*) is justified.

The meaning is that while you, who are like a helmsman, remain awake, a sinking of the earth into the waters—like that of a boat—is not possible. Here, because the superimposition of the state of being a helmsman upon the Blessed One serves the purpose of the contextual matter at hand, namely the prevention of the earth’s sinking, there is the figure of speech *pariṇāma* (transformation); this is further combined with the figure of speech *upamā* (simile). || 81 ||
With you as her girdle in the form of a jewel-belt, the ocean-girdled earth,
its afflictions caused by the demons having been pacified, deserves to be adorned.

Regarding the word *raśanā*: the Earth has the ocean as her girdle—that is, she is girt by the sea. By you, through the form of the jewel-girdle (the Kaustubha) which rests upon the ocean, she—who has had the affliction of the Danavas pacified—is worthy of adornment (*pariṣkaraṇa*). The sense is: "What is the use of adornment for one who is undergoing suffering? Having thus removed her suffering by the destruction of the Daityas, she is now fit to be adorned.

Regarding the statement in the *Amarakośa* commentary, “*nibhasaṃkāśanīkāśapratikāśopamādayaḥ*,” it is said that by the word "etc. (*ādi*), terms such as *bhūta*, *rūpaka*, and *kalpa* are included; thus, the word *rūpa* here signifies "similarity. For this very reason, there is the poetic figure of *upamopakrama-utprekṣā*. However, if it were to denote its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), then the superimposition (*āropa*) of the "jewel" upon the "girdle" would serve the purpose of the act of adornment, resulting in the poetic figure of *pariṇāma*. || 82 ||
May this earth long remain as a crest-ornament for you, who are the very form of Śeṣa, with Kaṃsa and the others extracted like thorns. 83.

"Kaṃse" (O Kaṃsā)! Thus experiencing suffering—this earth is present here, as if with arrows whose shafts have entered within and been extracted; [extracted] for a long time by you, who are of the nature of Śeṣa, from Kaṃsa and others. Let there be a crest-lock (*śikhaṇḍaka*)—that is, a tuft of hair like a crow's wing—for you. The meaning is: "The earth, having attained lightness through the destruction of the Daityas, may become easy to carry, like a crest-lock of Śeṣa."

By this, it is indicated that even for Śeṣa there was a great burden in the destruction of the Daityas. There is a conjunction (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) of the simile (*upamā*) "like arrows" and the metaphor (*rūpaka*) "crest-jewel. Through the phrase "by Kaṃsa and others who were extracted," there is an injunction of a qualified cause; according to the principle of "he offers with curd," this results in an injunction of the qualifier. Thus, what is intended here is that the very extraction of Kaṃsa and the others constitutes the cause for his being easily borne. (83)
Quickly drench us with your side-glances, which are lovely through their awakening [of consciousness], smiling, serene, and cool—the very waves of the singular ocean of compassion. (84)

He awakens [them]. By means of awakening—that is, by the departure of the sleep of yoga—he [is endowed with] beautiful eyes; Yādava states: “*Cakṣuṣya* means lovely because of its beauty. [The eyes are] serene, accompanied by the play of the eyebrows and a gentle smile. The definition [of such a gaze] is: “That is serene which is accompanied by the play of the eyebrows and is smiling” (BP 5). They are smiling, blossoming with joy, and—metaphorically—cool, because they remove the suffering of the multitude of devotees.

May compassion alone—the primary ocean—quickly flood and drench us with its waves, namely its side-long glances. Here, because the metaphorical representation of compassion as an ocean and the metaphorical representation of side-long glances as waves arise in succession, there is the poetic figure of *paramparita-rūpaka* (successive metaphor). || 84 ||
{1}: I have the following reading: "That [glance] should be gracious, accompanied by the play of the eyebrows and a smile.

Another reading: "Quickly drench us with side-glances that are gracious, delightful through their awakening [of consciousness], smiling, and cool—[glances that are] like the waves of the singular ocean of compassion."
"You ought to forgive this mockery of a petition from us, who have entrusted our burden to you—you, for whom all that is to be known is already known.

(85) Regarding the word "tvayi" (*in you*): "of us, who have entrusted our burden to you" means those who have performed the act of seeking refuge by surrendering their responsibility. "Of us" refers to ourselves. "For whom all that is to be known is already known"—the word "your" is to be supplied. "This mockery of a petition" refers to this very request, which is an improper action. "You" [should] "forgive" it; you ought to pardon it. (85)
Another reading: "Since we have entrusted our burden to you, you ought to forgive this mockery of a petition from those who know all that is to be known."
While the Creator was speaking thus in the assembly of the gods, the Earth paid homage to the Lord, who had undertaken the vow to protect Vinatā.

(86) Regarding the word *ittham*: while [the Creator] was speaking thus (*ittham*) in the assembly (*samāje*), that is, in the gathering (*samūhe*) of the gods, together with the Creator (*vedhasā*), that is, with Brahmā—while he was speaking thus—the Earth (*pṛthivī*) paid homage (*vavande*) to the Lord (*devam*), who was consecrated (*dīkṣitam*), that is, who had undertaken the vow (*kṛtavratam*), for the protection (*trāṇe*) of Vinatā. (86)
Another reading: *saha vedhasā* (together with the Creator).
The slender-waisted, large-eyed, slim woman with full breasts was like a great illusion, a jewel among women, belonging to him [the King] along with the Creator. (87)

"She with the slender waist" (*tanumadhyā*): *tanvī* means one with delicate limbs; *tanumadhyā* means she who is even more slender in her middle portion. "Large-eyed" (*viśālākṣī*) means long-eyed. "Possessing full breasts" (*pīnapayodharā*) means having swelling bosoms. "A jewel among women" (*vanitāratnam*) means the best of women; for Amara states: "The word *ratna* also refers to the most excellent of its own kind. She is so described because she possesses that form. She stood like the great *māyā* (illusion) of that Blessed One.
Because of her exceedingly enchanting form, she is to be imagined as "the great *māyā* of Viṣṇu personified. The connection with the preceding verse is "she paid homage" (*vavande*). || 87 ||
She bore the splendor of a peacock-feather parasol, effortlessly obtained by swarms of bees who were infatuated with the fragrance of her tresses.

"Ābaddha" means bound. "Alakāḥ" refers to curly locks of hair; Amara states: "Alakāḥ are curls of hair" (AK 2.5.721). By those [bees] who are deluded—that is, rendered helpless—by their fragrance, or scent; for this very reason, by bees moving about having formed circles, that is, having formed a circle and wandering around. Bearing, without effort, the splendor of a peacock-feather parasol—the beauty of a canopy made of peacock feathers—which was obtained effortlessly.

“‘The terms *lakṣmī*, *śrī*, *kānti*, and *saṃpat* are also employed in the sense of beauty,’ says Halāyudha. Here, the carrying of peacock-umbrellas, which is appropriate for the queens of the king, has been performed by the bees; thus, because the bees—referred to with different case endings—are transformed into the form of peacock-umbrellas, there is the figure of speech known as *vyadhikaraṇapariṇāma* (transformation with a different substratum). || 88 ||
Her breasts were adorned with drops of tears born from the joy of seeing her beloved,
which served as a decorative arrangement of pearls.

"Priyā" (the beloved). With her breasts adorned by drops of tears produced by the joy arising from the sight of her beloved—tears for which pearl ornaments have been set, meaning they are fashioned as if they were pearl decorations—the line of those very drops of joyful tears is here identified with the pearl ornaments on her breasts. Thus, the figure of speech is *atiśayokti* (hyperbole) in the form of identity (*abheda-rūpa*), wherein there is a distinction [between the actual tears and the imagined pearls] that is treated as non-distinction. || 89 ||
The right hand greatly esteemed the left arm, which was throbbing as if desiring the embrace of her beloved.

"Throbbing" means: throbbing intensely, as if desiring the embrace of her beloved—she who was skilled (dakṣiṇā), meaning proficient in discerning the signs of good and evil fortune. For one who hastens with excessive longing indeed wanders about and does not remain still in one place. "The other than the right" means the left arm; she considered it as being "much" (bahu). And for women, the left side is superior, while for men, it is the right.

"Because of the Smṛti text: 'In giving, in the worship of gods and others, in movement, and even in adorning oneself,' [the touch] was highly esteemed for its auspicious indication; thus, because of the attribution of a desire for an embrace upon his arm, there is the figure of speech known as *utprekṣā* (poetic fancy). || 90 ||
Another reading: She considered her right arm to be far superior to the other, as it throbbed, longing for an embrace of her beloved.
And this sweet-voiced lute spoke of misfortune, its pearl-like teeth and coral-like lower lip obscured by an embarrassed smile. (91)

"Vipadam" means: like a *vipañcī* lute, she possesses a sweet voice and a heart-pleasing sound; this is the Earth. "Vilakṣasmitam" means a smile accompanied by wonder; Amara states: "One who is possessed of wonder is *vilakṣa*" (AK 3.1.53). Or, it may mean a smile accompanied by shame. For, according to the definition: "He in whom a great sense of bashfulness (*apatrapā*) arises when his own lapse is correctly perceived by others is known as *vilakṣa*"—this [definition] is impossible here, because a specific type of shame cannot serve as the defining characteristic for its general category.

She, whose lower lip was like coral (*vidruma*) and from which pearls were scattered by her embarrassed smile—she being thus described as "one possessing a scattering of pearls"—spoke of her calamity. The word *ca* (and) serves to aggregate the action with that of the preceding verse. Here, there is a simile (*upamā*) in the phrase "the lute with its sweet sound," and a metaphor (*rūpaka*) because the smile is represented as pearls and the lower lip as coral; thus, there is a conjunction (*saṃsṛṣṭi*) of these two figures. || 91 ||
Then the Blessed One replied to them with auspicious words,
which were made resonant by the echoing sound of the Pāñcajanya conch.

"Then" (atha) means immediately after the words of Dharaṇī. "The Blessed One" (bhagavān). By "auspicious" (bhavyayā), meaning beautiful; by "resonance" (pratiśrut), meaning an echo; by "of that which has attained a roar" (prāptanirhrādasya), meaning of the Pāñcajanya, the conch of the Blessed One; by "to be rejoiced in" (abhinandyayā)—the sense is that she remained as if being greeted by the Pāñcajanya itself, which possessed that very resonance. This is an implied poetic fancy (gamyo-tprekṣā). By such a voice, he addressed those gods. Through the fact that it was caused by an echo, the extreme profundity of the Blessed One's voice is revealed. || 92 ||
"Do not fear the army of the Asuras, for you have me as your refuge.
For those who do not disregard my command, there shall be no humiliation. (93)

"Do not fear. Those for whom I am the refuge and protection are "those who have me as their refuge" (*madupāśrayāḥ*). O sirs! From the army of the Asuras—that is, from the host of the Daityas—do not fear; do not be terrified. Because of the connection with the word *bhavat*, there is an absence even of the original base (*sthānin*) when *yuṣmad* is the subordinate term (*upapada*), and thus the first person is used according to the rule: "In the remaining cases, the first person [is used]" (*śeṣe prathamaḥ*). [The phrase] "of one who does not disregard my command" means one whose habit is to transgress my commands. This suffix *tṛn* is used in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*).

In connection with that [term], because the genitive case is prohibited by the rule *na lokāvyaya* (Pāṇini 2.3.69) and others, the accusative case is used in *madājñām*. *Paribhūtyā* means "by way of humiliation. *Na bhūyate* is in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāve*), using the present tense (*laṭ*). The meaning is that for those who follow my command, no humiliation occurs from any quarter. In *mā bhaiṣuḥ*, the suffix *luṅ* is applied to the root *ñibhī* (to fear). Due to its conjunction with *mā*, there is an absence of the augment *aṭ*.

Since the meaning of the subsequent sentence functions as the cause for the sense of *mā bhaiṣuḥ*, the poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is *vākyārthahetuka-kāvyaliṅga* (poetic causality based on the meaning of the entire sentence). || 93 ||
O immortals, having descended as my incarnation to remove the burden of the earth,
he will establish the eternal and indestructible Dharma.

"Descend," [it says]. O immortals! My descent shall be for the purpose of removing the burden of the earth—the burden of the Daityas. He will establish the unimpaired Dharma, which is without beginning or end and has proceeded in a uniform manner through the flow of infinite time. || 94 ||
As long as you enjoy your desired pleasures and remain in office, protect your own positions, free from misfortune. 95.

"Yāvat" means: "vigatāpadaḥ" (free from calamity) refers to those whose calamities have been removed once the Daityas have been destroyed by my descent. "Yāvadiṣṭabhujaḥ" means enjoying as much as desired; the sense is that they enjoy as many sacrifices and other rites as they desire. And while remaining "yāvadadhikāram" (for as long as their office lasts), "paripālayata" (protect) your own "padāni" (stations or positions). In the compounds "yāvadiṣṭam" and "yāvadadhikāram," the term "yāvat" is used in the sense of limitation (avadhāraṇe), according to Pāṇini’s rule [Pāṇini 2.1.8]. || 95 ||
O lords of the thirty gods, by the subduing of the lords of the Danujas,
you shall behold the earth once again restored to its lightness, as if it had been cured of disease.

"Because of the subduing. O lords of the thirty-three gods, O best of deities! Because of the subduing of the lords of the Danujas, the foremost of the Asuras, you shall once again behold the earth—having attained lightness as before—as if it were cured of its ailment, made free from disease. "Ullāgha means one who has emerged from illness," according to Amara. The word *ullāghita* is derived from the root *ullāgh*, with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) meaning "to make [something] so," followed by the past passive participle suffix (*niṣṭhā*) in the sense of the object. 96.
Even you must become lords of men upon this earth, sharing in the pleasure of the hunt amidst throngs of Daitya deer. (97)

"O Daityas! [He says: "Even by you, on this earth, there must be kings who partake in the sentiment (*rasa*) and the curiosity (*kautuka*) of the hunt—the hunt being the expedition against the herds of deer that are none other than the Daityas, the Asuras. The meaning is: 'You too must descend into the Kṣatriya lineages for the sake of slaying certain wicked ones.

The word *bhāgin* is derived from the root *bhaj* with the suffix *ghinuṇ* according to the rule beginning with *saṃpṛcānurudha* (Pāṇini 3.2.142), and the substitution of *k* for *j* occurs by the rule *ca joḥ ku ghiṇṇyatoḥ* (Pāṇini 7.3.52). || 97 ||
Having thus instructed them, Janārdana, whose command is faultless,
set his mind upon Mathurā, disregarding the Ocean of Milk.

"Thus" (*iti*) means: Janārdana, whose commands are unimpeded (*anaghādeśa*), having thus instructed those gods, disregarded the Ocean of Milk—that is, having set aside the Milky Ocean—he fixed his mind upon Mathurā; the meaning is that he desired, "I must descend to Mathurā, leaving the Ocean of Milk behind. This accords with the statement in the *Bhāgavata*: "This glorious Nārāyaṇa, whose abode is the Ocean of Milk, has indeed left his serpent-couch and come to the city of Mathurā" (MBh 3.86.20). || 98 ||
Having comforted the sons of Aditi with showers of the nectar of his speech, as well as the Goddess Earth who was bowed down by the burden of the Daityas,
the sinless Lord of Lakṣmī, desiring to manifest in the wife of Vasudeva, fixed his mind upon the time for his compassionate descent.

Now, in accordance with the definition "in every case [the verses end] with distinct creations" (*sarvatra bhinnasargāntaiḥ*), he describes another episode at the conclusion of the creation, beginning with the words "having consoled" (*āśvāsya*). "Anaghaḥ" means faultless; that is, being subject to various individual karmas, He is free from the defects of partiality and cruelty. "Padmāpatiḥ" means the Lord of Śrī. "Vāgevāmṛtam" means speech itself is nectar; by its "showers" (*vṛṣṭibhiḥ*). "Āditeyān" refers to the gods, who are the offspring of Aditi.

From the word *aditi*, the form is derived by adding the suffix *ṅīṣ* according to the rule *“kṛdikārād aktinaḥ”* and then adding the suffix *ḍhak* according to the rule *“strībhyo ḍhak”*. The word *daiteya* is formed in the same manner. Having consoled the goddess Earth, who was bowed down by the weight of the Daityas, and desiring to manifest himself (*prādurbubhūṣuḥ*)—that is, wishing to appear—in Devakī, the wife of Vasudeva, he fixed his mind upon the occasion for compassion; that is, he reflected upon the proper time.

The meaning is that he waited for the appropriate time according to their respective karmas, out of compassion for the living beings oppressed by the asuras and for Devakī and Vasudeva. This verse is composed in the meter known as Vasantatilakā. || 99 ||

Desirous of establishing the stainless foundation of Dharma for the virtuous who are like bees at the lotuses of his own feet, he—whose womb contains the entire universe and who is worshipped by the gods of gods—was born as the embryo of Devakī. 100.

“Of the virtuous” (*sādhūnām*). “The entire world” (*akhilaṃ jagat*) is that which is within his womb—that which resides in his belly. According to the *Vaijayantī* lexicon, which provides various meanings: “*garbhaḥ* [is used] for the belly (*kukṣi*) and for a creature residing in the belly (*kukṣisthite jantau*). He is the one who is to be saluted even by the gods of the gods, such as Brahmā and others; he alone is Vāsudeva. To the virtuous who are attached to his own foot—just as bees (*ṣaṭpadānām*) are to a lotus (*saroja*)—he grants the stability of dharma, that is, its proper boundary (*maryādām*).

Desirous of creating—that is, wishing to bring forth—the sinless and faultless one, he was born as the embryo of Devakī; that is, he was produced. Regarding the root *jan*, the suffix *ciṇ* is applied in the sense of the agent in the *luṅ* tense by the rule "dīpajana" (Pāṇini 3.1.61). In the compound *vidhātukāmaḥ*, it is a *bahuvrīhi*: "one whose desire is to create," or alternatively, "one possessing the desire to create. The compound belongs to the *mayūravyaṃsakādi* class. The elision of the *m* is according to the rule "tuṃ kāmamanasor api" (Vārttika on Pāṇini 6.1.144).

Ātreya maintains that the reading *daivakī*—meaning "the offspring of Devaka"—is correct according to the rule for *vṛddhi* [vowel strengthening]. However, the form without *vṛddhi* is more widely known. Furthermore, the usage is seen in the *Yamakaratnākara*: "He who is the creator of this entire world, whose mother is Devakī; he whose source of bliss here is his incarnations, and whose mother is Devakī. (n.i.)

Even though it ends in the suffix *aṇ*, the absence of *vṛddhi* is possible, as in the case of *jyotis*, because the rule for *vṛddhi* is non-universal (*anitya*) due to its being a technical injunction (*saṃjñāpūrvaka*). In the phrase "svapadasaroja" (the lotus of one's own words), there is the figure of speech known as *paraṃparitarūpaka* (successive metaphor). This verse is composed in the *praharṣiṇī* meter. || 100 ||

Thus ends the first canto in the great poem *Yādavābhyudaya*, composed by the illustrious Veṅkaṭanātha, the Vedāntācārya, the lion among poets and logicians, who is independent in all philosophical systems.

Regarding the word *iti*: the first *iti* denotes completion and is connected with the phrase "the first canto" (*prathamaḥ sargaḥ*). "Poets" (*kavayaḥ*) are those who compose poetry. "Logicians" (*tārkikāḥ*) are disputants who sport with logic; the suffix *ṭhak* is applied according to the rule *tena divyati*. Of those who act as adversaries to the lion, or of that which is as terrifying as a lion among them, or of the best among them—Amara states: "The words *siṃha*, *śārdūla*, *nāga*, and so forth, when used in the masculine, refer to excellence. (Amarakośa 3.1.121).

Among all the tantras and established doctrines—namely the Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Pūrva- and Uttara-mīmāṃsā, Sāṅkhya, Yoga, Śaiva, Vaiṣṇava, and others—he is the independent Vedāntācārya, the teacher of the secret meaning of Vedānta, the illustrious Veṅkaṭanātha, who is capable of establishing or refuting any point according to his own will. The locative case [in the original] is used in the sense of selection from among many, according to the rule *yataś ca nirdhāraṇe* (Pāṇini 2.3.41); thus, the meaning is "among the compositions written by him."

In the *Yādavābhyudaya*, which was composed concerning the rise (*abhyudaya*) of Kṛṣṇa, the descendant of Yadu—the suffix *aṇ* prescribed by the rule *“adhikṛtya kṛte granthe”* [Pāṇini 4.3.87] has been elided by the rule *“lub ākhyāyikābhyo bahulam”* [Pāṇini 4.3.87]. This work is a literary composition (*prabandha*) endowed with the characteristics of a *mahākāvya* as stated [in the *Śārṅgadharapaddhati*]: “It consists of cantos that are not overly extensive, contains verses easy to recite, possesses well-formed junctures (*saṃdhi*), and throughout is characterized by distinct endings to each canto; it is intended to delight the world.
This is the first canto; the meaning is that it is thus completed.

Thus ends the first canto in the *Yādavābhyudayavyākhyāna* composed by Appayya Dīkṣita, the son of the eminent sacrificial priest Śrī Raṅgarājādhvarin— the Kaustubha jewel of the ocean that is the illustrious Bhāradvāja lineage, and the performer of the Viśvajit sacrifice.
Salutation to the illustrious teacher of Vedānta.
